name: Zuph
title: Levite ancestor of Samuel the prophet
bio: Zuph, also called Zophai, was an Ephraimite Levite, an ancestor of Samuel the prophet.

name: Hannah
title: The mother of the prophet Samuel.
bio: Hannah was the wife of Elkanah, an Ephraimite, and the mother of the prophet Samuel (1 Samuel 1:1). She was one of Elkanah's two wives, the other being Peninnah. While Peninnah had children, Hannah was barren, which caused her great distress (1 Samuel 1:2). During an annual visit to the tabernacle at Shiloh, Hannah prayed fervently to the Lord, asking for a son and vowing to dedicate him to the Lord's service (1 Samuel 1:9). Eli, the high priest, initially mistook her intense prayer for drunkenness but later blessed her when he understood her situation (1 Samuel 1:12). In due time, Hannah conceived and gave birth to a son, whom she named Samuel, meaning "heard by God" (1 Samuel 1:19). After weaning him, Hannah fulfilled her vow and brought Samuel to the tabernacle to serve under Eli (1 Samuel 1:24). Hannah's prayer of thanksgiving (1 Samuel 2:1) expresses her joy and gratitude for God's answer to her prayers and her recognition of God's sovereignty. The Bible also records that Hannah had three more sons and two daughters after dedicating Samuel to the Lord (1 Samuel 2:21). Hannah's story illustrates the power of prayer, faith, and dedication to God.

name: Peninnah
title: Elkanah's wife, rival of Hannah
bio: Peninnah, one of Elkanah's two wives and the rival of Hannah, Samuel's mother.
meaning: [poss.] pearls, coral branches; woman with rich hair

name: Eli
title: High priest and judge of Israel at Shiloh
bio: Eli, a prominent figure in 1 Samuel, served as the high priest and judge of Israel at the tabernacle in Shiloh. He first appears in the narrative when Hannah, the mother of Samuel, prays at the tabernacle (1 Samuel 1:9). Eli initially misunderstands her prayer but later blesses her. After Samuel's birth, Hannah dedicates him to serve under Eli at the tabernacle (1 Samuel 1:25). However, Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were wicked and did not follow God's ways (1 Samuel 2:12). Eli failed to restrain their behavior, leading to a prophecy of judgment against his family (1 Samuel 2:27). Eli continued to serve as the high priest and judge, while Samuel grew up in the tabernacle (1Samuel 3). In his old age, Eli received news of Israel's defeat by the Philistines, the capture of the Ark of the Covenant, and the death of his sons. Upon hearing this, Eli fell backward, broke his neck, and died at the age of 98 (1 Samuel 4:12). His death marked the end of an era and the beginning of Samuel's leadership as a prophet and judge.
meaning: y-h-v-h is exalted; G-d [El] is exalted

name: Hophni
title: A corrupt priest, son of Eli.
bio:
Hophni was one of the two sons of Eli, the high priest of Israel, who served at the tabernacle in Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:3). Along with his brother Phinehas, Hophni was known for his corrupt behavior and disregard for the proper handling of the sacrifices and offerings brought to the tabernacle (1 Samuel 2:12). 

The corrupt practices of Hophni and Phinehas led to the people's disillusionment with the priesthood and a decline in the spiritual life of Israel. As a consequence of their actions, a prophecy was given to Eli, stating that both of his sons would die on the same day (1 Samuel 2:34). 

During a battle against the Philistines, the Israelites brought the Ark of the Covenant from Shiloh to the battlefield, accompanied by Hophni and Phinehas (1 Samuel 4:4). However, the Israelites were defeated, the Ark was captured, and both Hophni and Phinehas were killed, fulfilling the prophecy (1 Samuel 4:11). When Eli heard the news of his sons' deaths and the capture of the Ark, he fell backward from his seat, broke his neck, and died (1 Samuel 4:17). 

The story of Hophni serves as a warning against the abuse of religious authority and the consequences of disobedience to God's laws. It also highlights the importance of proper worship and the handling of sacred objects in maintaining a right relationship with God.

name: Phinehas
title: Wicked son of Eli the priest
bio:
Phinehas was one of the two sons of Eli, the priest who served in the tabernacle at Shiloh (1 Samuel 1:3). Along with his brother Hophni, Phinehas was described as a worthless man who did not know the Lord (1 Samuel 2:12). They abused their priestly duties by taking more than their share of the sacrificial meat and engaging in sexual immorality with the women who served at the entrance of the tabernacle (1 Samuel 2:13). 

Eli rebuked his sons for their wicked behavior, but they did not listen (1 Samuel 2:22). As a result, a prophecy was given to Eli that his two sons would die on the same day (1 Samuel 2:34). This prophecy was fulfilled when the Philistines defeated the Israelites in battle, captured the Ark of the Covenant, and killed Hophni and Phinehas (1 Samuel 4:11). Upon hearing the news of his sons' deaths and the capture of the Ark, Eli fell backward, broke his neck, and died (1 Samuel 4:17). Phinehas' wife, who was pregnant, went into labor and died after giving birth to a son named Ichabod, which means "the glory has departed from Israel" (1 Samuel 4:19).

name: Samuel
title: Prophet and last judge of Israel before the kings

elkanah.note: Named in the same passage, but Scripture doesn't state this word for word.

hannah.note: Read from the wording of the verse, which doesn't fix the relationship exactly.

bio:
Samuel was a prophet and the last judge of Israel before the establishment of the monarchy. He was born to Hannah, who had been barren, and dedicated to the Lord's service from birth (1 Samuel 1:11). Samuel grew up in the tabernacle under the guidance of Eli the priest (1 Samuel 2:18). God called Samuel while he was still a boy, and he became a prophet (1Samuel 3). Samuel played a crucial role in Israel's transition from the period of the judges to the monarchy. He led Israel in a decisive victory over the Philistines at Mizpah (1 Samuel 7:5) and served as a judge over Israel (1 Samuel 7:15). When the people demanded a king, Samuel anointed Saul as the first king of Israel (1Samuel 8-10). However, when Saul disobeyed God, Samuel announced that God had rejected him as king (1Samuel 15). Samuel then anointed David as the next king (1 Samuel 16:1). Samuel continued to guide and counsel David, even when Saul pursued him (1 Samuel 19:18). After Samuel's death, he was buried in Ramah (1 Samuel 25:1). He is remembered as a faithful prophet and judge who played a pivotal role in Israel's history (Psalm 1 Samuel 99:6; Jeremiah 15:1; Acts 3:24; Hebrews 11:32). 

In 1 Chronicles 6:33 he is listed in the genealogy of the Levites, specifically in the line of Kohath, which was one of the three main divisions of the Levites (1 Chronicles 6:1). This Samuel is an ancestor of Heman, who was one of the chief musicians appointed by David to lead worship in the tabernacle (1 Chronicles 6:31). It is important to note that this Samuel is not the same person as the prophet and judge Samuel, who was also the son of an Elkanah (1 Samuel 1:20). The Samuel mentioned in 1 Chronicles 6:33 lived much earlier than the prophet Samuel and was part of the Levitical line that served in the tabernacle and temple worship.

name: Abijah

bio: Abijah was one of Samuel's sons who served as a judge in Israel but did not follow his father's righteous ways.

name: Joel
title: Samuel's firstborn son who judged Israel
bio: Joel was the firstborn son of the prophet and judge Samuel, as mentioned in 1 Samuel 8:2. Along with his brother Abijah, Joel was appointed by Samuel to serve as a judge in Israel. However, unlike their father, Joel and Abijah did not walk in the ways of the Lord. They turned aside after dishonest gain, accepted bribes, and perverted justice (1 Samuel 8:3). This corruption in leadership led the elders of Israel to demand a king to rule over them, ultimately resulting in the anointing of Saul as the first king of Israel (1 Samuel 8:4). The failure of Joel and Abijah to uphold the standards of righteous judgment set by their father had significant consequences for the nation of Israel.

name: Abiel
title: Father of Kish and grandfather of King Saul
bio:
Abiel, also referred to as Jeiel, Ner, or Abigibeon (or '[re]-founder of Gibeon'), was a Benjaminite and the father of Kish, who was the father of King Saul, Israel's first king. In 1 Samuel 9:1, Abiel is mentioned as the father of Kish and is described as a mighty man of power. The genealogies in 1Chronicles 8 and 9 provide additional information about Abiel's family. 

In 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 1 Chronicles 9:39, he is called Ner, while in 1 Chronicles 8:29 and 1 Chronicles 9:35, he is referred to as Jeiel and Abigibeon or '[re]-founder of Gibeon'. These variations in names suggest that he may have been known by multiple names or that there might have been some discrepancies in the genealogical records. Abiel's son Kish became the father of Saul, who was anointed as the first king of Israel by the prophet Samuel.

name: Aphiah
title: Ancestor of King Saul, a Benjamite
bio: Aphiah, a Benjamite, was an ancestor of King Saul, the first king of Israel.

name: Becorath
title: An ancestor of King Saul from the tribe of Benjamin.
bio: Becorath was an ancestor of King Saul and a member of the tribe of Benjamin.

name: Kish
title: Father of Saul, the first king of Israel

abiel-1.note: 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 9:39 say Ner fathered Kish. TIPNR reads that Ner as another name for Abiel, because 1 Samuel 14:51 makes Kish and Abner's father Ner brothers.

maacah-6.note: Named in the same passage, but Scripture doesn't state this word for word.

benjamin.note: Read from the wording of the verse, which doesn't fix the relationship exactly.

bio:
Kish, a Benjamite from the family of Matri, was the father of Saul, the first king of Israel. He is introduced in 1 Samuel 9:1 as a wealthy and influential man. Kish's donkeys went missing, and he sent his son Saul and a servant to search for them (1 Samuel 9:3). This journey led to Saul's meeting with the prophet Samuel, who anointed him as king over Israel (1 Samuel 10:1). 

Kish is mentioned several times in the context of Saul's kingship. He was present when Saul was chosen by lot as king at Mizpah (1 Samuel 10:21). Later, when Saul faced a Philistine threat, some people questioned his ability to lead, referring to him as "the son of Kish" (1 Samuel 10:11). 

Kish's family background is further elaborated in the genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:30). These passages confirm Kish as the father of Saul and provide details about his ancestors and descendants. 

After Saul's death, David honored the remains of Saul and his son Jonathan by burying them in the tomb of Kish at Zela (2 Samuel 21:14). This act demonstrates David's respect for Saul's family and his desire to bring closure to the tragic events surrounding Saul's reign. 

In the New Testament, the Apostle Paul, in his speech at Antioch, mentions Kish as the father of Saul when recounting the history of Israel (Acts 13:21). 

Throughout the biblical narrative, Kish is primarily known as the father of Saul, the first king of Israel. His life and influence are closely tied to the rise and reign of his son, and his legacy is remembered in the context of Israel's early monarchy.

name: Zeror
title: Ancestor of King Saul
bio: Zeror, a Benjamite, was an ancestor of King Saul.

name: Saul
title: First king of Israel, anointed by Samuel
bio: Saul was the first king of Israel, anointed by the prophet Samuel in response to the people's request for a king (1Samuel 8-10). He was a tall and handsome Benjamite who initially showed humility and potential as a leader (1 Samuel 9:2). However, Saul's reign was marked by disobedience and rebellion against God. He offered an unlawful sacrifice before a battle against the Philistines (1 Samuel 13:8) and later disobeyed God's command to completely destroy the Amalekites and their possessions (1Samuel 15). As a result, God rejected Saul as king and chose David to replace him (1 Samuel 15:23). Saul became jealous of David's success and popularity, leading him to pursue David and attempt to kill him on multiple occasions (1Samuel 18-26). Saul also massacred the priests of Nob for assisting David (1 Samuel 22:6). In a battle against the Philistines, Saul was critically wounded and took his own life to avoid capture (1 Samuel 31:1). His body was later recovered by the men of Jabesh-gilead and buried (1 Samuel 31:11). Despite his tragic end, Saul's reign united the tribes of Israel and laid the foundation for the Israelite monarchy. His life serves as a warning against disobedience and the consequences of turning away from God.

name: Matri
title: Saul's ancestral clan from the tribe of Benjamin.
bio: The Matrite (or Matri) clan was Saul's ancestral clan from the tribe of Benjamin.

name: Nahash
title: Ammonite king who besieged Jabesh Gilead.
bio: Nahash, the king of the Ammonites, besieged Jabesh Gilead and threatened to gouge out the right eyes of its inhabitants.

name: Jonathan
title: Eldest son of King Saul and friend of David

ahinoam-1.note: Named in the same passage, but Scripture doesn't state this word for word.

bio:
Jonathan was the eldest son of King Saul and a prominent figure in the early monarchy of Israel. He first appears in the biblical narrative as a brave warrior, leading a thousand men in a successful attack against a Philistine garrison (1 Samuel 13:2). Jonathan's faith and courage were further demonstrated when he and his armor-bearer challenged another Philistine outpost, believing that God could save by many or by few (1 Samuel 14:6). 

Jonathan is perhaps best known for his deep friendship with David, which began after David's victory over Goliath (1 Samuel 18:1). The two made a covenant, and Jonathan gave David his robe, armor, sword, bow, and belt as a sign of their bond (1 Samuel 18:3). When Saul's jealousy towards David grew, Jonathan interceded on David's behalf, temporarily reconciling them (1 Samuel 19:1). 

As Saul's hostility towards David intensified, Jonathan helped David escape and reaffirmed their covenant (1Sa.20). They parted ways, with Jonathan remaining loyal to his father while still maintaining his friendship with David (1 Samuel 23:16). 

Jonathan died in battle alongside his father and brothers at Mount Gilboa, fighting against the Philistines (1 Samuel 31:2; 1 Chronicles 10:2). David deeply mourned the loss of his friend, composing a lament in honor of Saul and Jonathan (2Sa.1). 

Jonathan's legacy continued through his son Mephibosheth, whom David showed kindness for Jonathan's sake (2 Samuel 4:4; 9.1-7). David also spared Mephibosheth's life when the Gibeonites sought retribution for Saul's actions (2 Samuel 21:7). 

The story of Jonathan and David's friendship has become a timeless example of loyalty, selflessness, and the power of covenant relationships. Despite the challenges and conflicts they faced, their bond remained strong, transcending political and familial ties.

name: Ahimelech
title: High Priest at Nob who helped David, killed by Saul
bio:
Ahimelech, also known as Ahijah, was the priest at Nob during the reign of King Saul. He was the son of Ahitub and the father of Abiathar. When David was fleeing from Saul, he came to Ahimelech at Nob seeking help. Ahimelech, unaware of the conflict between David and Saul, provided David with the consecrated bread and the sword of Goliath. (1 Samuel 21:1) 

Doeg the Edomite, one of Saul's servants, witnessed this interaction and reported it to Saul. Saul summoned Ahimelech and the other priests, accusing them of conspiring with David against him. Despite Ahimelech's defense of his actions, Saul ordered the execution of the priests. Doeg carried out the order, killing Ahimelech and eighty-four other priests. (1 Samuel 22:9). 

Abiathar, Ahimelech's son, was the only one who escaped the massacre. He fled to David and brought with him the ephod, a priestly garment used for seeking God's guidance. (1 Samuel 22:20; 23.6; 30.7) 

The story of Ahimelech's tragic fate is also referenced in Psalm 52, which is attributed to David when Doeg informed Saul about Ahimelech's assistance to David. The psalm reflects on the consequences of those who trust in evil and contrasts them with those who trust in God's steadfast love. (Psalm 52:0)

name: Ahitub
title: Father of Ahimelech, High Priest at Nob killed by Saul

phinehas_eli.note: Read from the wording of the verse, which doesn't fix the relationship exactly.

bio:
Ahitub was the father of Ahimelech, who served as the priest at Nob during the reign of King Saul. Ahitub's other son, Ahijah, also served as a priest and wore an ephod, indicating his priestly role. (1 Samuel 14:3). He is not specifically named as a High Priest but he is the gradson of High Priest Eli and father of High Priest Ahimelech.  

When David fled from Saul, he came to Ahimelech at Nob seeking help. Ahimelech provided David with the consecrated bread and the sword of Goliath. (1 Samuel 21:1) However, Doeg the Edomite, one of Saul's servants, witnessed this interaction and reported it to Saul. (1 Samuel 22:9). 

Saul summoned Ahimelech and the other priests, accusing them of conspiring with David against him. Despite Ahimelech's defense of his actions, Saul ordered the execution of the priests. Doeg carried out the order, killing Ahimelech, along with eighty-four other priests who were from the family of Ahitub. (1 Samuel 22:11) 

Only Abiathar, Ahimelech's son, escaped the massacre and fled to David, bringing with him the ephod. (1 Samuel 22:20) The tragedy that befell Ahitub's family highlights the tension between Saul and David and the consequences faced by those caught in the middle of their conflict.

name: Abinadab
title: Son of King Saul, killed in battle

ahinoam-1.note: Named in the same passage, but Scripture doesn't state this word for word.

bio:
Abinadab, also referred to as Ishvi, was one of the sons of King Saul, the first king of Israel (1 Samuel 14:49; 1 Chronicles 8:33). He was the brother of Jonathan, Malchishua, and Esh-baal (also known as Ish-bosheth). 

Abinadab fought alongside his father and brothers in the battle against the Philistines at Mount Gilboa. In this battle, Saul and his sons, including Abinadab, were killed (1 Samuel 31:2; 1 Chronicles 10:2). The Philistines found their bodies the following day and fastened Saul's body to the wall of Beth-shan, while the bodies of his sons were taken to Jabesh-gilead and buried there (1 Samuel 31:8). 

The death of Abinadab and his brothers marked the end of Saul's reign and paved the way for David to become king over Israel.
meaning: [my] father is generous or [my] father is Nadab

name: Malchi-shua
title: Son of King Saul, killed in battle against the Philistines.

ahinoam-1.note: Named in the same passage, but Scripture doesn't state this word for word.

bio: Malchi-shua was one of the sons of King Saul, the first king of Israel. He was a brother of Jonathan, Abinadab, and Ishvi. Malchi-shua fought alongside his father and brothers in the battles against the Philistines. In a fierce battle on Mount Gilboa, the Philistines overwhelmed the Israelite army. Malchi-shua, along with his brothers Jonathan and Abinadab, was killed in the battle. King Saul, upon seeing his sons dead and facing imminent capture, took his own life by falling on his sword (1 Samuel 14:49; 1 Chronicles 8:33).

name: Merab
title: Eldest daughter of King Saul.

ahinoam-1.note: Named in the same passage, but Scripture doesn't state this word for word.

bio: Merab was the eldest daughter of King Saul (1 Samuel 14:49). She was initially promised to David as a wife, with the condition that he fight valiantly for Saul and the Lord (1 Samuel 18:17). However, when the time came for her to be given to David, she was instead given to Adriel the Meholathite as a wife (1 Samuel 18:19). Merab had five sons with Adriel, and these sons were among the seven descendants of Saul who were handed over to the Gibeonites for execution, as a means of atonement for Saul's attempt to annihilate the Gibeonites (2 Samuel 21:8). This event occurred during David's reign, when a three-year famine prompted David to seek the Lord's guidance.

name: Michal
title: Daughter of Saul; wife of David.

ahinoam-1.note: Named in the same passage, but Scripture doesn't state this word for word.

bio: Michal was the younger daughter of King Saul and became the first wife of David, Israel's future king. She first appears in the genealogy of Saul (1 Samuel 14:49) and is later mentioned as loving David (1 Samuel 18:20). Saul, seeking to ensnare David, offered Michal's hand in marriage, demanding a bride price of 100 Philistine foreskins. David fulfilled this requirement, and Michal became his wife (1 Samuel 18:27). When Saul attempted to kill David, Michal helped him escape through a window and deceived Saul's messengers by placing an idol in David's bed (1 Samuel 19:11). During David's exile, Saul gave Michal in marriage to Palti (1 Samuel 25:44). After Saul's death, David demanded that Michal be returned to him as a condition for peace with Abner (2 Samuel 3:13). Later, when David danced before the ark of the Lord, Michal despised him in her heart (2 Samuel 6:16; 1 Chronicles 15:29). She confronted David, criticizing his behavior, but David rebuked her (2 Samuel 6:20). As a result, Michal remained childless until her death (2 Samuel 6:23). Michal's story illustrates the complex relationships and conflicts within Saul's family and the early years of David's rise to power.

name: Abner
title: Saul's cousin and commander of his army
bio:
Abner was the son of Ner and the cousin of King Saul, Israel's first monarch. He served as the commander of Saul's army (1 Samuel 14:50). Abner was a prominent figure during Saul's reign and demonstrated his loyalty to the king, as seen in his interactions with David (1 Samuel 17:55). 

After Saul's death, Abner supported Saul's son Ish-bosheth as king over Israel, while David reigned over Judah (2 Samuel 2:8). During this time, there was a long war between the houses of Saul and David (2 Samuel 3:1). Abner led Ish-bosheth's forces against David's army, commanded by Joab (2 Samuel 2:12). In a battle at Gibeon, Abner killed Joab's brother Asahel, who had pursued him (2 Samuel 2:18). 

Later, Abner defected to David after a dispute with Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 3:6). He worked to transfer the kingdom to David and made an agreement with him (2 Samuel 3:12). However, Joab, seeking revenge for his brother's death, murdered Abner (2 Samuel 3:22). David mourned Abner's death and declared his innocence in the matter (2 Samuel 3:28). 

Abner's defection and death weakened Ish-bosheth's position, and he was eventually assassinated (2 Samuel 4:1). This paved the way for David to become king over all Israel (2 Samuel 5:1). David later reminded Solomon of Joab's actions against Abner (1 Kings 2:5). Abner is also mentioned in connection with the treasures dedicated to the Lord (1 Chronicles 26:28) and as the father of Jaasiel, a leader in David's army (1 Chronicles 27:21).

name: Ahimaaz
title: Father of Saul's wife Ahinoam
bio: Ahimaaz was the father of Ahinoam, who was the wife of King Saul.

name: Ahinoam
title: Wife of King Saul, daughter of Ahimaaz
bio: Ahinoam, the daughter of Ahimaaz, was one of King Saul's wives.

name: Ner
title: Father of Abner, King Saul's commander.

abiel-1.note: Read from the wording of the verse, which doesn't fix the relationship exactly.

maacah-6.note: Named in the same passage, but Scripture doesn't state this word for word.

bio:
Ner was an important figure in the early history of Israel's monarchy, primarily known as the father of Abner, the commander of King Saul's army. He was a member of the tribe of Benjamin and a close relative of Saul, as evidenced by the fact that Saul and Abner are referred to as sons of Ner (1 Samuel 14:50). 

Although little is known about Ner's life, his significance lies in his family's connection to the first king of Israel, Saul. As the father of Abner, Ner's lineage played a crucial role in the political and military leadership of Israel during Saul's reign. 

Abner, as the commander of Saul's army, is mentioned several times in the biblical narrative, particularly in the context of the conflict between Saul and David (1 Samuel 26:5). After Saul's death, Abner supported Saul's son, Ish-bosheth, as king over Israel, while David was anointed as king over Judah (2 Samuel 2:8). 

The tension between Abner and David's forces is evident in the accounts of their military encounters (2 Samuel 2:12). However, Abner eventually defected to David's side after a falling out with Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 3:6). Tragically, Abner was later killed by Joab, David's commander, in an act of revenge for the death of Joab's brother (2 Samuel 3:22). 

David mourned Abner's death and publicly declared his innocence in the matter (2 Samuel 3:31). The incident with Abner is also mentioned in the context of Solomon's reign, as David instructed Solomon to deal with Joab for his role in Abner's murder (1 Kings 2:5). 

Ner is also briefly mentioned in genealogical records, such as in 1 Chronicles 9:36, where he is listed among the ancestors of Saul, and in 1 Chronicles 26:28, which notes that some of the dedicated treasures in the temple were from the days of Samuel, Saul, Abner, and Joab. 

Although Ner himself is not the primary focus of the biblical narrative, his family's connection to Saul and the early monarchy of Israel makes him a significant figure in the historical context of the Old Testament.

name: Agag
title: Amalekite king captured and killed by Samuel
bio:
Agag was the king of the Amalekites during the reign of King Saul of Israel. God commanded Saul to attack the Amalekites and totally destroy everything, including Agag. Saul defeated the Amalekites but spared Agag and the best of the livestock. The prophet Samuel rebuked Saul for his disobedience and told him that God had rejected him as king. Samuel then summoned Agag and "hewed him in pieces before the Lord." (1 Samuel 15:8) 

The book of Esther mentions that Haman, the enemy of the Jews, was an Agagite, which suggests he may have been a descendant of Agag the Amalekite. (Esther 3:1; 8.3,5; 9.24).

name: Eliab
title: Eldest brother of King David
bio: Eliab, mentioned in 1 Samuel 16:6; 1 Chronicles 2:13; and 2 Chronicles 11:18, was the eldest son of Jesse and the brother of King David. When the prophet Samuel came to anoint one of Jesse's sons as the future king, Eliab was the first to pass before him. However, God instructed Samuel not to judge by appearance, as He had not chosen Eliab (1 Samuel 16:6). Eliab, along with his brothers, served in Saul's army during the battle against the Philistines. When David visited the camp, Eliab rebuked him, accusing him of neglecting their father's sheep out of pride and curiosity (1 Samuel 17:28). Despite this tension, Eliab witnessed David's victory over Goliath and his rise to prominence in Israel. Eliab's daughter, Abihail, later married King Rehoboam, the son of Solomon (2 Chronicles 11:18), indicating a continued connection between the families.

name: Abinadab
title: Son of Jesse, brother of David
bio: Abinadab was one of the sons of Jesse and an older brother of King David, but he was not chosen to be anointed as king by Samuel.
meaning: [my] father is generous or [my] father is Nadab

name: Shimeah
title: Brother of David; father of Jonadab (or 'Jonathan').
bio: Shimeah, also referred to as Shimei, Shammah, or Shimea, was one of King David's brothers (1Ch. 2:13). He was the son of Jesse and is mentioned in the genealogy of Judah. Shimeah had a son Jonadab (or 'Jonathan'). Jonathan is described as a skilled warrior who killed a Philistine giant (2Sa. 21:21; 1Ch. 20:7), while Jonadab is portrayed as a crafty man who helped Amnon, David's son, to deceive and rape his half-sister Tamar (2Sa. 13:3, 32).

name: Goliath
title: A Philistine giant defeated by David.

rapha-2sa-21-16.note: 2 Samuel 21:22: "These four were descended from Rapha in Gath."

bio: Goliath was a Philistine warrior from the city of Gath who fought against the Israelites during the reign of King Saul. He is described as a giant, standing at six cubits and a span (approximately 9 feet 9 inches or 3 meters) tall, and wearing heavy bronze armor (1 Samuel 17:4). Goliath challenged the Israelites to send a champion to face him in single combat, but no one dared to accept the challenge until David, a young shepherd, volunteered. With a sling and a stone, David defeated Goliath, striking him on the forehead and killing him (1 Samuel 17:48). David then cut off Goliath's head with the giant's own sword (1 Samuel 17:51). This event is significant in David's life, as it marked the beginning of his rise to prominence in Israel. The sword of Goliath was kept as a trophy, and David later retrieved it from the tabernacle at Nob when he was fleeing from Saul (1 Samuel 21:9:10). In 2 Samuel 21:19 and 1 Chronicles 20:5, there is mention of another Goliath, also from Gath, who was killed by Elhanan, one of David's warriors. Some scholars believe this may refer to a brother or relative of the Goliath killed by David.

name: Adriel
title: Saul's son-in-law; husband of Merab
bio: Adriel married Saul's daughter Merab and had five sons.

name: Doeg
title: Edomite chief shepherd who betrayed David to Saul
bio:
Doeg the Edomite was a chief shepherd in the service of King Saul. He first appears in 1 Samuel 21:7, where he is described as the chief herdsman of Saul and is present at the tabernacle in Nob when David arrives seeking help from the priest Ahimelech. 

Later, in 1Samuel 22, Doeg plays a crucial role in the events that follow. When Saul learns that Ahimelech had assisted David, he summons the priests to appear before him. Doeg, being present at the time, informs Saul that he had seen David receiving help from Ahimelech (1 Samuel 22:9). 

Acting on Saul's orders, Doeg kills 85 priests who were wearing the linen ephod, as well as the entire city of Nob, including men, women, children, and livestock (1 Samuel 22:18). This massacre highlights Doeg's ruthless obedience to Saul and his willingness to carry out violent acts against innocent people. 

Doeg's actions are condemned in Psalm 52, which is attributed to David. The psalm describes Doeg as a deceitful and evil man who loves falsehood and delights in destruction (Psalm 1 Samuel 52:1). The psalmist expresses confidence that God will bring judgment upon Doeg and that the righteous will ultimately prevail (Psalm 1 Samuel 52:5). 

Doeg's story serves as an example of the dangers of misplaced loyalty and the consequences of aligning oneself with those who oppose God's chosen leaders. His betrayal of David and his role in the massacre at Nob stand in stark contrast to the faithfulness and righteousness exemplified by David and Ahimelech.

name: Achish
title: Philistine king of Gath, gave refuge to David
bio:
Achish, also known as Abimelech, was the Philistine king of Gath during the time of King Saul and King David. When David fled from Saul, he sought refuge in Gath, pretending to be insane to avoid being perceived as a threat (1 Samuel 21:10). Achish's servants recognized David as the celebrated Israelite warrior, but David's act of insanity convinced Achish to dismiss him (1 Samuel 21:11). 

Later, when David was again fleeing from Saul, he returned to Achish in Gath, this time with a group of 600 men (1 Samuel 27:1). Achish granted David and his men the town of Ziklag as a base (1 Samuel 27:5). David and his men raided the Geshurites, Girzites, and Amalekites, but deceived Achish into believing that they were raiding the Israelites and their allies (1 Samuel 27:8). 

When the Philistines gathered their forces to fight against Israel, Achish brought David and his men with him (1 Samuel 28:1). However, the Philistine commanders objected to David's presence, fearing that he might turn against them in battle (1 Samuel 29:1). Achish, trusting in David's loyalty, defended him, but ultimately sent him back to Ziklag (1 Samuel 29:6). 

After David became king, some of his servants fled to Achish in Gath (1 Kings 2:39), indicating that David maintained a relationship with Achish even after becoming king. 

Psalm 34 is attributed to David when he pretended to be insane before Abimelech (Achish), who drove him away (Psalm 1 Kings 34:1). The psalm expresses David's trust in God and his deliverance from fear and trouble.

name: King of Moab
title: King of Moab to whom David took his parents (1 Samuel 22:3)

name: Gad
title: Prophet during the reigns of David and Solomon.
bio: Gad was a prophet who served during the reigns of King David and his son Solomon. He first appears in 1 Samuel 22:5, where he advises David to leave his stronghold in Moab and return to the land of Judah. Gad played a significant role in the events surrounding David's census of Israel (2Samuel 24; 1Chronicles 21). After David had sinned by taking the census, Gad was sent by God to offer David a choice of three punishments: three years of famine, three months of fleeing from enemies, or three days of plague (2 Samuel 24:11; 1 Chronicles 21:9). David chose the plague, and Gad instructed him to build an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite to stop the plague (2 Samuel 24:18; 1 Chronicles 21:18). Gad is described as David's seer (2 Samuel 24:11; 1 Chronicles 21:9) and is credited with writing a book about David's acts (1 Chronicles 29:29). He was also involved in organizing the music and worship in the tabernacle (2 Chronicles 29:25). Gad's ministry as a prophet spanned the latter years of David's reign and continued into the early years of Solomon's reign.

name: Abiathar
title: High priest during the reigns of David and Solomon
bio: Abiathar was the son of Ahimelech, a priest at Nob. When King Saul ordered the execution of the priests at Nob, Abiathar was the only one who escaped and fled to David (1 Samuel 22:20). He brought with him the ephod, a sacred priestly garment used for seeking God's will (1 Samuel 23:6). Abiathar remained loyal to David throughout his reign, serving as one of his chief priests (2 Samuel 8:17). However, near the end of David's life, Abiathar supported Adonijah's attempt to become king instead of Solomon (1 Kings 1:7). When Solomon became king, he removed Abiathar from the priesthood, fulfilling the prophecy against the house of Eli (1 Kings 2:26). Abiathar is also mentioned in the New Testament by Jesus, who referred to an incident during Abiathar's time as high priest (Mark 2:26).
meaning: [my] father gives abundance or the father is preeminent

name: Abigail
title: Wife of Nabal, later married David
bio:
Abigail was a wise and beautiful woman who was initially married to a wealthy but foolish man named Nabal. When David and his men were in the wilderness, Nabal refused to provide them with food and supplies. Abigail, learning of this, quickly gathered provisions and went to meet David, apologizing for her husband's behavior and urging David not to seek revenge. 

Impressed by her wisdom and courage, David accepted her appeal and spared Nabal's life. When Abigail told Nabal about this incident, he had a heart attack and died ten days later. After Nabal's death, David sent for Abigail and married her. 

Abigail became one of David's wives and bore him a son named Chileab, who is also known as Daniel (2 Samuel 3:3; 1 Chronicles 3:1). She accompanied David during his time in Ziklag, where he sought refuge from King Saul (1 Samuel 27:3). Abigail's story demonstrates her wisdom, diplomacy, and faith in God.
meaning: [my] father rejoices or father [cause] of joy

name: Nabal
title: Wealthy Carmelite; husband of Abigail. He was known for foolishness.
bio:
Nabal was a wealthy man from Carmel who lived during the time of King David. He is described as a Calebite, indicating his descent from the tribe of Judah. Nabal was married to Abigail, a beautiful and intelligent woman (1 Samuel 25:3). 

Despite his wealth, Nabal was known for his harsh and foolish behavior. When David and his men, who had been protecting Nabal's shepherds and flocks, requested provisions, Nabal rudely refused, insulting David and his men (1 Samuel 25:4). This foolish act provoked David to seek revenge, threatening to kill Nabal and all the males in his household. 

Abigail, upon learning of her husband's foolishness, quickly intervened. She gathered a generous supply of food and went out to meet David, apologizing for Nabal's behavior and pleading for mercy (1 Samuel 25:18). Her wise actions and words appeased David, who relented from his plan to attack Nabal's household. 

When Abigail informed Nabal of how close he had come to disaster, his heart failed him, and he became like a stone. About ten days later, the Lord struck Nabal, and he died (1 Samuel 25:36). After Nabal's death, David sent for Abigail and married her (1 Samuel 25:39). 

Nabal's story serves as a cautionary tale about the consequences of foolishness, selfishness, and mistreating others. It also highlights the wisdom and courage of Abigail, who acted decisively to protect her household and make peace with David.

name: Ahinoam
title: Wife of David, from Jezreel; mother of Amnon
bio:
Ahinoam of Jezreel was one of the wives of King David. She became David's wife after he fled from King Saul and settled in the wilderness of Paran. (1 Samuel 25:43) Ahinoam accompanied David during his time in Ziklag, a city given to him by Achish, the king of Gath. (1 Samuel 27:3) 

When the Amalekites raided Ziklag and took captive the women and children, including Ahinoam, David pursued the raiders and rescued all who had been captured. (1 Samuel 30:5). 

After Saul's death, David and his wives, including Ahinoam, moved to Hebron, where David was anointed king over Judah. (2 Samuel 2:2) Ahinoam gave birth to David's firstborn son, Amnon, in Hebron. (2 Samuel 3:2; 1 Chronicles 3:1) 

As one of David's wives, Ahinoam held an important position in the royal household. However, the biblical text does not provide further details about her life or her relationship with David beyond her role as the mother of Amnon.

name: Laish
title: Father of Michal's husband Palti (or 'Paltiel')
bio: Laish, the father of Palti (or 'Paltiel'), to whom Saul gave his daughter Michal in marriage.

name: Palti
title: Michal's husband from Gallim
bio: Palti (Paltiel), son of Laish, was Michal's husband from Gallim before she was taken back by David.

name: Abishai
title: David's nephew, one of his mighty men and commanders

husband-of-zeruiah-1sa-26-6.note: Read from the wording of the verse, which doesn't fix the relationship exactly.

bio:
Abishai was the son of Zeruiah, King David's sister, making him David's nephew (1 Chronicles 2:16). He was the brother of Joab and Asahel, two other prominent figures in David's military ranks (2 Samuel 2:18). Abishai was one of David's mighty men and a trusted commander in his army. 

During David's flight from King Saul, Abishai accompanied him and showed his loyalty by offering to kill Saul when they found him sleeping in the camp (1 Samuel 26:6). However, David refused to allow Abishai to harm the Lord's anointed (1 Samuel 26:9). 

Abishai played a significant role in many of David's military campaigns. He fought alongside Joab against Abner and the forces of Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 2:24). After Abner killed Asahel, Joab and Abishai pursued him but were convinced to halt their pursuit (2 Samuel 2:24). Later, Abishai supported Joab in avenging Asahel's death by killing Abner (2 Samuel 3:30). 

In the battle against the Ammonites, Abishai led a division of the army and helped secure victory for Israel (2 Samuel 10:10; 1 Chronicles 19:11). He also accompanied David during the rebellion of Absalom and was one of the three commanders of David's forces (2 Samuel 18:2). 

Abishai intervened to save David's life when a giant named Ishbi-benob threatened to kill the king (2 Samuel 21:17). He was also known for his bravery and military exploits, being credited with killing three hundred men with his spear (2 Samuel 23:18; 1 Chronicles 11:20). 

Throughout David's reign, Abishai remained a loyal and trusted commander, playing a crucial role in maintaining David's kingdom and defending Israel against its enemies.
meaning: [my] father is Jesse or father exists

name: Ahimelech
title: Son of Ahitub, a Hittite warrior who joined David
bio: Ahimelech the Hittite was one of David's warriors who accompanied him to Saul's camp while Saul was pursuing David.

name: Joab
title: Son of Zeruiah, commander of David's army

husband-of-zeruiah-1sa-26-6.note: Read from the wording of the verse, which doesn't fix the relationship exactly.

bio:
Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was King David's nephew and the commander of his army. He first appears in 1 Samuel 26:6, accompanying David on a mission to Saul's camp. Joab played a significant role in David's rise to power and the establishment of his kingdom (2Sa.2-3; 8.16; 1 Chronicles 11:6). 

As a military commander, Joab led David's forces in various battles against the Ammonites, Syrians, and other enemies (2Sa.10; 12.26-27; 1Ch.19). He also helped quell Absalom's rebellion and was instrumental in defeating Sheba's revolt (2Sa.18; 20). 

However, Joab's loyalty to David was sometimes overshadowed by his own ambition and ruthlessness. He killed Abner, Saul's former commander, in revenge for his brother Asahel's death (2Sa.3). He also disobeyed David's orders by killing Absalom (2Sa.18) and supported Adonijah's attempt to seize the throne (1 Kings 1:7). 

Despite his flaws, Joab remained a key figure in David's reign until the end. He was involved in the census that brought God's judgment upon Israel (2Sa.24; 1Ch.21) and was eventually killed by Benaiah on Solomon's orders for his support of Adonijah (1 Kings 2:28).

name: Zeruiah
title: Sister of David; mother of Joab, Abishai, and Asahel

jesse.note: Named in the same passage, but Scripture doesn't state this word for word.

bio: Zeruiah was the sister of King David and the mother of three of his most prominent military leaders: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel. Her sons played significant roles throughout David's reign, both in military campaigns and in political matters. Joab served as the commander of David's army, while Abishai and Asahel were also known for their bravery and skill in battle. Zeruiah's sons were fiercely loyal to David, though their actions sometimes brought them into conflict with the king. For example, Joab murdered Abner and Amasa, two of David's rivals, without the king's consent. Despite these tensions, David recognized the importance of Zeruiah's sons in establishing and maintaining his kingdom. The fact that Zeruiah is consistently mentioned as their mother highlights her significance in the family and her influence on her sons' roles in David's court.

name: Husband of Zeruiah
title: Husband of Zeruiah; father of Abishai and Joab
bio: The unnamed husband of Zeruiah, who was the father of David's mighty men, Abishai and Joab.

name: Maoch
title: Father of Achish, king of Gath.
bio: Maoch (or Maacah) was the father of Achish, king of Gath, to whom David fled.

name: Ish-bosheth
title: Son of Saul, king over Israel.
bio:
Ish-bosheth, also known as Eshbaal, was the fourth son of King Saul (1 Chronicles 8:33.39). After Saul's death, Abner, the commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth and made him king over Israel, while David reigned over Judah (2 Samuel 2:8). Ish-bosheth was forty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned for two years. 

During his reign, there was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David (2 Samuel 3:1). Abner became angry with Ish-bosheth and defected to David (2 Samuel 3:8). Later, two of Ish-bosheth's captains, Rechab and Baanah, assassinated him while he was resting in his bed. They brought his head to David, hoping for a reward, but David had them executed for their crime (2 Samuel 4:5). 

After Ish-bosheth's death, all the tribes of Israel came to David and acknowledged him as king over all Israel (2 Samuel 5:1). The name "Ish-bosheth" means "man of shame," while "Eshbaal" means "man of Baal." The name change may reflect the biblical writer's perspective on the contrast between Ish-bosheth's weak rule and David's divinely appointed kingship.

name: Asahel
title: Son of Zeruiah, brother of Joab, killed by Abner

husband-of-zeruiah-1sa-26-6.note: 2 Samuel 2:32: Asahel was buried in his father's tomb in Bethlehem. Scripture doesn't name his father.

bio: Asahel was the youngest son of Zeruiah, David's sister, and the brother of Joab and Abishai. He was known for his speed and agility, being described as fleet-footed as a wild gazelle. During the battle between the forces of David and Ish-Bosheth at Gibeon, Asahel pursued Abner, the commander of Ish-Bosheth's army. Despite Abner's warnings to turn aside, Asahel refused, and Abner killed him with the butt of his spear. Joab and Abishai later avenged their brother's death by murdering Abner when he came to support David. Asahel was one of David's mighty men and was placed in charge of a division in David's army.

name: Amnon
title: David's firstborn son, killed by Absalom
bio:
Amnon was the firstborn son of King David, born to him in Hebron. His mother was Ahinoam of Jezreel. Amnon is primarily known for his infamous act of raping his half-sister Tamar, who was the sister of Absalom. After the incident, Amnon's love for Tamar turned to hatred, and he sent her away in shame. 

Absalom, enraged by Amnon's actions, waited two years before exacting revenge. He invited Amnon to a sheep-shearing feast and had his servants kill Amnon when he was drunk. This led to a rift between Absalom and his father, David, and ultimately to Absalom's rebellion against the king. The story of Amnon highlights the tragic consequences of sexual violence and the far-reaching effects it can have on families and relationships.

name: Absalom
title: David's rebellious son who tried to usurp the throne.
bio:
Absalom was the third son of King David, born to Maacah, the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur (2Sa. 3:3). He was known for his handsome appearance and long hair (2Sa. 14:25-26). After the rape of his sister Tamar by Amnon, David's firstborn son, Absalom plotted revenge and had Amnon murdered (2Sa. 13). He then fled to Geshur for three years before Joab, David's general, arranged for his return (2Sa. 14). 

Later, Absalom launched a rebellion against David, proclaiming himself king in Hebron (2Sa. 15). David was forced to flee from Jerusalem, and Absalom took advice to pursue him with his forces (2Sa. 16-17). However, David's men defeated Absalom's army, and Absalom himself was killed by Joab against David's wishes (2Sa. 18). David deeply mourned Absalom's death (2Sa. 19:1-4). 

Absalom had erected a pillar to preserve his name, since he had no son to carry on his lineage (2Sa. 18:18). He was survived by his daughter Maacah, who later became a wife of Rehoboam and mother of Abijah (1Ki. 15:2; 2Ch. 11:20-21).

name: Chileab
title: Son of David and Abigail the Carmelitess

abigail.note: Read from the wording of the verse, which doesn't fix the relationship exactly.

bio: Chileab, also known as Daniel, was David's son by Abigail the Carmelitess.

name: Maacah
title: Daughter of Talmai; wife of David; mother of Absalom
bio: Maacah, the daughter of King Talmai of Geshur, was one of David's wives and the mother of Absalom.

name: Talmai
title: King of Geshur; father of David's wife Maacah

name: Adonijah
title: Son of David who attempted to seize the throne

david.note: Read from the wording of the verse, which doesn't fix the relationship exactly.

bio:
Adonijah was the fourth son of King David, born to him in Hebron (2 Samuel 3:4; 1 Chronicles 3:2). He was the son of Haggith and was born after Absalom, who had also rebelled against David. 

When King David was old and frail, Adonijah exalted himself, declaring, "I will be king" (1 Kings 1:5). He prepared chariots, horses, and fifty men to run before him, and he conferred with Joab, the commander of the army, and Abiathar the priest, who followed and supported him. However, he did not invite Nathan the prophet, Benaiah, the mighty men, or his brother Solomon to his coronation (1 Kings 1:7). 

Nathan, aware of Adonijah's actions, advised Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, to inform David and remind him of his oath to make Solomon king after him. David, upon hearing this, confirmed his choice of Solomon and ordered his anointing and proclamation as king (1 Kings 1:11). 

When Adonijah and his supporters heard that Solomon had been anointed king, they fled in fear. Adonijah took hold of the horns of the altar, seeking protection. Solomon spared his life on the condition that he would show himself to be a worthy man (1 Kings 1:50). 

However, after David's death, Adonijah made a request through Bathsheba to be given Abishag the Shunammite, who had been David's companion in his old age, as his wife. Solomon perceived this request as a claim to the throne and ordered Benaiah to execute Adonijah (1 Kings 2:13). 

Adonijah's story serves as a warning against ambition and rebellion, highlighting the importance of submitting to God's chosen leadership and the consequences of seeking power through illegitimate means.

name: Haggith
title: One of David's wives; mother of Adonijah.
bio: Haggith was one of King David's wives and the mother of Adonijah, who was David's fourth son (2 Samuel 3:4 Chronicles 2 Samuel 3:2). Adonijah was born in Hebron during the early years of David's reign. After the death of his older brothers Amnon and Absalom, Adonijah considered himself the heir to the throne and attempted to claim it while David was still alive (1 Kings 1:5). He gained the support of Joab, the commander of the army, and Abiathar, the priest (1 Kings 1:7). However, David had promised Bathsheba that their son Solomon would be the next king (1 Kings 1:17). When David was informed of Adonijah's actions, he ordered Solomon to be anointed as king (1 Kings 1:32). Fearing for his life, Adonijah sought asylum by clinging to the horns of the altar (1 Kings 1:50). Solomon spared his life on the condition that he would show himself to be a worthy man (1 Kings 1:52). Later, Adonijah made a request to Solomon through Bathsheba, asking for Abishag, David's nurse, to be given to him as a wife (1 Kings 2:13). Solomon perceived this as a threat to his throne and ordered Adonijah to be put to death (1 Kings 2:23).
meaning: festal; born on the feast day

name: Aiah
title: Father of Rizpah, Saul's concubine
bio:
Aiah is mentioned in the Bible as the father of Rizpah, a concubine of King Saul. Rizpah had two sons with Saul, named Armoni and Mephibosheth. (2 Samuel 21:8) 

After Saul's death, Abner, the commander of Saul's army, had relations with Rizpah, which was considered a challenge to the authority of Saul's son and successor, Ish-bosheth. This led to a conflict between Abner and Ish-bosheth. (2 Samuel 3:7). 

Later, during the reign of King David, a famine struck Israel for three years. The Lord revealed that it was due to Saul's bloodguilt against the Gibeonites. To make amends, David handed over seven of Saul's descendants, including Rizpah's two sons, to the Gibeonites, who killed them. (2 Samuel 21:1) 

Rizpah then took sackcloth and spread it on a rock, guarding the bodies of her sons and the other five men from the beginning of harvest until the rains came. She protected them from scavenger birds during the day and wild animals at night. (2 Samuel 21:10) 

When David heard about Rizpah's actions, he was moved and ordered the retrieval of the bones of Saul, Jonathan, and the seven men who had been killed. They were buried in the tomb of Saul's father, Kish, and after that, God answered the prayers for the land. (2 Samuel 21:11) 

Aiah's daughter, Rizpah, demonstrated remarkable courage, loyalty, and maternal love in her actions, which ultimately led to the proper burial of Saul and his descendants.

name: Rizpah
title: Concubine of Saul; mother of Armoni and Mephibosheth
bio: Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah, was a concubine of King Saul (2 Samuel 3:7). She bore Saul two sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 21:8). After Saul's death, Abner, the commander of Saul's army, had relations with Rizpah, which was seen as a challenge to the authority of Saul's son and successor, Ish-bosheth (2 Samuel 3:7). Years later, during the reign of King David, a famine struck Israel for three years (2 Samuel 21:1). The Lord revealed that the famine was a consequence of Saul's attempt to kill the Gibeonites, with whom Israel had made a treaty (2 Samuel 21:1; Joshua 9:3). To make atonement, the Gibeonites demanded the execution of seven of Saul's male descendants, including Rizpah's sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 21:5). Rizpah displayed great devotion and grief by protecting the bodies of her sons from birds and wild animals, staying with them from the beginning of the harvest until the rains came (2 Samuel 21:10). When David heard of Rizpah's actions, he ordered the proper burial of the bones of Saul, Jonathan, and the seven executed men (2 Samuel 21:11). Rizpah's story highlights the tragic consequences of Saul's disobedience and the depths of a mother's love and grief in the face of loss.

name: Baanah
title: A captain who murdered Ish-bosheth, Saul's son.
bio: Baanah was one of the two captains who assassinated Ish-bosheth, the son of King Saul. After Saul's death, Ish-bosheth had been proclaimed king over Israel, while David ruled over Judah. According to 2Samuel 4, Baanah and his brother Rechab, who were Benjamites from Beeroth, entered Ish-bosheth's house while he was resting and killed him. They brought his head to David, hoping to be rewarded. However, David condemned their treacherous act and ordered their execution. The text describes Baanah and Rechab as wicked men who murdered an innocent person. Their actions were motivated by self-interest rather than loyalty. David's response demonstrated his integrity and respect for Saul's family, as he refused to condone violence against his rivals.

name: Rechab
title: A captain of Ishbosheth's army, with his brother Baanah
bio: Rechab is mentioned in 2 Samuel as the brother of Baanah, both captains in the army of Ishbosheth, the son of Saul (2 Samuel 4:2). After the death of Saul, Ishbosheth was made king over Israel, while David reigned over Judah (2 Samuel 2:8). Baanah and Rechab, who were from the tribe of Benjamin, betrayed Ishbosheth by sneaking into his house while he was resting and murdering him (2 Samuel 4:5). They brought Ishbosheth's head to David, hoping to gain favor with him (2 Samuel 4:8). However, David condemned their treacherous act and ordered their execution (2 Samuel 4:9). The actions of Rechab's sons contributed to the downfall of Ishbosheth and the eventual unification of Israel under David's rule. The story highlights the political instability and violence that characterized the early days of David's reign.
meaning: [prob.] rider or horseman [from to ride, mount]

name: Rimmon

bio: Rimmon was a Beerothite and the father of Rechab and Baanah, who murdered Ish-bosheth, Saul's son.

name: Mephibosheth
title: Son of Jonathan and grandson of King Saul.
bio: Mephibosheth, also known as Merib-baal, was the son of Jonathan and grandson of King Saul (1 Chronicles 8:34; 9.40). He was five years old when his father and grandfather died in battle at Mount Gilboa (2 Samuel 4:4). During the panic following their deaths, Mephibosheth's nurse picked him up to flee, but he fell and became lame in both feet (2 Samuel 4:4). Years later, when David had established his kingdom, he sought to show kindness to Mephibosheth for the sake of his father Jonathan (2 Samuel 9:6). David restored to him all the land that had belonged to Saul and allowed him to eat at the king's table regularly (2 Samuel 9:6). Mephibosheth had a young son named Mica (2 Samuel 9:12). During Absalom's rebellion, Mephibosheth's servant Ziba falsely accused him of disloyalty to David (2 Samuel 16:1). After Absalom's death, Mephibosheth met David and explained that Ziba had deceived him (2 Samuel 19:24). David divided Saul's land between Mephibosheth and Ziba (2 Samuel 19:30). Later, when the Gibeonites demanded seven of Saul's descendants to avenge Saul's attempt to annihilate them, David spared Mephibosheth because of his oath to Jonathan (2 Samuel 21:7).
meaning: from the mouth of Shame [a derogatory name for Baal]”

name: Hiram
title: King of Tyre, ally of David and Solomon.
bio:
Hiram, also known as Huram, was the king of Tyre, a Phoenician city-state located on the Mediterranean coast north of Israel. He is mentioned in several passages in the Old Testament, primarily in connection with his alliances with King David and King Solomon of Israel. 

During David's reign, Hiram sent envoys to David and provided him with cedar logs, carpenters, and stonemasons to build his palace (2 Samuel 5:11; 1 Chronicles 14:1). This gesture demonstrated the friendly relationship between Tyre and Israel and Hiram's recognition of David's growing power and influence in the region. 

Hiram's alliance with Israel continued during the reign of Solomon, David's son. He played a significant role in the construction of the First Temple in Jerusalem by supplying Solomon with cedar and cypress logs, as well as skilled craftsmen (1Kings 5; 2 Chronicles 2:3). In exchange, Solomon provided Hiram with large quantities of wheat, barley, olive oil, and wine (1 Kings 5:11; 2 Chronicles 2:10). 

The two kings also collaborated on maritime expeditions, with Hiram sending his skilled sailors to join Solomon's fleet in voyages to Ophir, a region known for its wealth in gold and other precious items (1 Kings 9:27; 2 Chronicles 8:18). 

In addition to their trade and construction projects, Hiram and Solomon exchanged gifts and engaged in diplomatic relations (1 Kings 9:11; 2 Chronicles 8:2). Their friendship and cooperation were instrumental in the growth and prosperity of both Tyre and Israel during this period.

name: Jerusalem wives

name: Nathan
title: Son of David and Bathsheba, ancestor of Jesus.

bathsheba.note: Read from the wording of the verse, which doesn't fix the relationship exactly.

bio:
Nathan was one of the sons of King David and Bathsheba, born in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 5:14; 1 Chronicles 3:5). He was a younger brother of Solomon, who would succeed David as king. 

Although little is known about Nathan's life, his significance lies in his role as an ancestor of Jesus Christ. In the genealogy of Jesus recorded in the Gospel of Luke, Nathan is listed as a descendant of David and an ancestor of Joseph, the husband of Mary (Luke 3:31). 

The prophet Zechariah also mentions a future mourning in Jerusalem, where the family of the house of David and the family of Nathan will mourn separately (Zechariah 12:12). This suggests that the descendants of Nathan played a significant role in the history of Israel and were recognized as a distinct lineage within the house of David. 

As a son of David, Nathan would have been part of the royal family during a time when Israel was at its peak of power and influence. His inclusion in the biblical record, both in the historical narratives and in the genealogy of Jesus, highlights the importance of the Davidic lineage in God's plan of redemption.

name: Solomon
title: Son of David, king of Israel, known for his wisdom.
bio:
Solomon, also known as Jedidiah, was the son of King David and Bathsheba, and the third king of Israel (2 Samuel 12:24; 1 Chronicles 3:5). He was born in Jerusalem and named Solomon by his parents, but the prophet Nathan called him Jedidiah, which means "beloved of the Lord" (2 Samuel 12:25). 

Solomon ascended to the throne after his father David's death, following a power struggle with his older brother Adonijah (1Kings 1-2). As king, Solomon prayed for wisdom to govern his people, and God granted him exceptional wisdom, understanding, and knowledge (1 Kings 3:1; 2 Chronicles 1:1). His wisdom was demonstrated through his fair judgments, such as the famous case of the two women claiming the same baby (1 Kings 3:16). 

During his reign, Solomon undertook ambitious construction projects, most notably the building of the First Temple in Jerusalem, which took seven years to complete (1Kings 6; 2Chronicles 3-4). He also built a palace for himself, fortified cities, and established a strong military force (1Kings 7; 1 Kings 9:15; 2 Chronicles 8:1). 

Solomon's reign was marked by prosperity, wealth, and international recognition. He formed alliances with neighboring kingdoms, engaged in extensive trade, and received tribute from foreign rulers (1Kings 5; 2 Chronicles 9:26; 2 Chronicles 8:17). The Queen of Sheba visited Solomon to test his wisdom and left impressed by his knowledge and the splendor of his court (1 Kings 10:1; 2 Chronicles 9:1). 

However, Solomon's later years were marked by a decline in his faithfulness to God. He married many foreign women and allowed their religious practices to influence him, leading to the worship of false gods (1 Kings 11:1). As a result, God declared that the kingdom would be divided after Solomon's death (1 Kings 11:9). 

Solomon is traditionally credited with authoring several biblical books, including Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Solomon (Proverbs 1:1; Ecclesiastes 1:1; Song of Solomon 1:1). His wisdom and proverbs were widely celebrated and studied (1 Kings 4:29; Proverbs 1:1). 

After a reign of forty years, Solomon died and was succeeded by his son Rehoboam (1 Kings 11:41; 2 Chronicles 9:29). As prophesied, the kingdom was divided into the northern kingdom of Israel and the southern kingdom of Judah shortly after his death (1Kings 12; 2Chronicles 10).
