name: Martha
title: Sister of Mary and Lazarus, hosted Jesus.
bio: Martha was a woman from Bethany who, along with her siblings Mary and Lazarus, was a close friend of Jesus. When Jesus visited their home, Martha welcomed Him and busied herself with serving, while her sister Mary sat at Jesus' feet, listening to His teachings. Martha complained to Jesus that Mary was not helping her, but Jesus gently reminded her that Mary had chosen the better part by focusing on His words (Luke 10:38). Later, when Lazarus fell ill and died, Martha went out to meet Jesus and expressed her faith in Him, saying that if He had been there, her brother would not have died. Jesus reassured her that Lazarus would rise again and proclaimed Himself as the resurrection and the life (John 11:1). After Lazarus was raised from the dead, Martha served a meal for Jesus and His disciples, demonstrating her love and gratitude (John 12:2).

name: Mary
title: Sister of Martha and Lazarus, sat at Jesus' feet.
bio: Mary was a woman from Bethany, the sister of Martha and Lazarus, and a close friend of Jesus. When Jesus visited their home, Mary sat at His feet, listening intently to His teachings, while her sister Martha was busy serving. When Martha complained that Mary was not helping, Jesus commended Mary for choosing the better part by focusing on His words (Luke 10:39). After the death of Lazarus, Mary fell at Jesus' feet, expressing her grief and faith in Him. Jesus was deeply moved by her sorrow and wept with her before raising Lazarus from the dead (John 11:1). Later, during a meal at their home, Mary took a pound of expensive perfume and anointed Jesus' feet, wiping them with her hair. This act of devotion and love was criticized by Judas Iscariot, but Jesus defended her, stating that she had anointed Him for His burial (John 12:3).
meaning: [variously] bitterness; plump one; wished-for child; one who loves or is loved

name: Lazarus
title: Poor man in Jesus' parable of the rich man
bio: Lazarus is the name given to the poor man in Jesus' parable of the rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19). In the parable, Lazarus is described as a beggar covered with sores who longed to eat the crumbs falling from the rich man's table (Luke 16:20). When both men died, Lazarus was carried by angels to Abraham's side in heaven, while the rich man found himself in Hades, in torment (Luke 16:22). The rich man called out to Abraham, asking him to send Lazarus to dip his finger in water and cool his tongue (Luke 16:24). However, Abraham replied that a great chasm separated them and that it was impossible for anyone to cross from one side to the other (Luke 16:25). The parable emphasizes the reversal of fortunes in the afterlife and the importance of caring for the poor and needy in this life.

name: Zacchaeus
title: Tax collector who hosted Jesus in Jericho
bio: Zacchaeus, a wealthy tax collector, hosted Jesus in his home and experienced a transformative encounter.
meaning: y-h-v-h has remembered, [or perhaps] y-h-v-h remember

name: Nathanael
title: Disciple of Jesus, from Cana in Galilee.
bio:
Nathanael, also identified as Bartholomew in the Synoptic Gospels, was one of the twelve disciples of Jesus Christ. He is introduced in the Gospel of John when Philip, who had just begun following Jesus, found Nathanael and told him, "We have found the one Moses wrote about in the Law, and about whom the prophets also wrote—Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph" (John 1:45). 

Initially skeptical, Nathanael questioned, "Nazareth! Can anything good come from there?" (John 1:46). However, when Jesus saw Nathanael approaching, he declared, "Here truly is an Israelite in whom there is no deceit" (John 1:47). Surprised, Nathanael asked how Jesus knew him, to which Jesus replied that he had seen him under the fig tree before Philip called him (John 1:48). 

This revelation prompted Nathanael to confess, "Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel" (John 1:49). Jesus commended Nathanael's faith and promised that he would see even greater things, alluding to the miracles and divine revelations that would follow. 

Nathanael is mentioned again in John 21:2 as one of the disciples who went fishing with Peter after Jesus' resurrection. He was present when Jesus appeared to them on the shore of the Sea of Tiberias and performed the miraculous catch of fish. 

Although little is known about Nathanael's life beyond these brief mentions, his inclusion among the twelve disciples highlights his importance in Jesus' ministry. His initial skepticism and subsequent confession of faith demonstrate the transformative power of encountering Jesus and the depth of his commitment to following him. 

Tradition holds that Nathanael, under the name Bartholomew, went on to preach the gospel in various regions, including India and Armenia, where he is said to have been martyred for his faith.

name: Nicodemus
title: Pharisee who visited Jesus
bio: Nicodemus was a Pharisee and a member of the Jewish ruling council, the Sanhedrin (John 3:1). He came to Jesus at night, likely to avoid being seen, and engaged in a discussion about the need to be born again to enter the kingdom of God (John 3:1). Later, Nicodemus defended Jesus before the Sanhedrin, reminding them that the law required a person to be heard before being judged (John 7:50). After the crucifixion, Nicodemus brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes to anoint Jesus' body for burial, demonstrating his devotion to Jesus (John 19:39). Though initially coming to Jesus in secret, Nicodemus grew to be a follower of Christ.

name: Simon
title: Father of Judas Iscariot, the disciple who betrayed Jesus.
bio: Simon is mentioned in the Gospel of John as the father of Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve disciples of Jesus (John 6:71). He is not to be confused with Simon Peter or any other Simon mentioned in the New Testament. The only information provided about this Simon is his relationship to Judas Iscariot, the disciple who betrayed Jesus. The gospels do not give any further details about Simon's life, occupation, or character. His son, Judas Iscariot, is infamous for his betrayal of Jesus, which led to Jesus' arrest and crucifixion. Despite being one of the twelve chosen disciples, Judas conspired with the Jewish authorities to hand Jesus over to them for thirty pieces of silver (Matthew 26:14). Simon's role in the biblical narrative is limited to being the father of the disciple who betrayed Jesus, highlighting the tragic choice made by Judas Iscariot.
meaning: he has heard or obedient one

name: Lazarus
title: Brother of Mary and Martha; raised from the dead
bio: Lazarus was the brother of Mary and Martha, who lived in the village of Bethany (John 11:1). Jesus loved Lazarus and his sisters (John 11:5). When Lazarus fell ill, his sisters sent word to Jesus, but by the time Jesus arrived, Lazarus had been dead for four days (John 11:6). Jesus went to the tomb and called for Lazarus to come out, and Lazarus emerged, still wrapped in burial cloths (John 11:43). This miraculous sign led many to believe in Jesus (John 11:45). Later, Jesus visited Lazarus' home, where Martha served a meal and Mary anointed Jesus' feet with perfume (John 12:1). The chief priests plotted to kill Lazarus because his resurrection caused many to believe in Jesus (John 12:9). Lazarus' story demonstrates Jesus' power over death and foreshadows His own resurrection.

name: Malchus
title: High priest's servant whose ear was cut off by Peter.
bio: Malchus, the high priest's servant, had his ear cut off by Peter during Jesus' arrest.

name: Daughter of Annas
title: The wife of Caiaphas the high priest.

annas.note: Read from the wording of the verse, which doesn't fix the relationship exactly.

bio: A reference to the unnamed wife of Caiaphas, the high priest who condemned Jesus.

name: Joseph
title: Candidate to replace Judas as apostle
bio: Joseph, also called Barsabbas or Justus, was considered as a replacement for Judas among the apostles.

name: Matthias
title: Apostle chosen to replace Judas Iscariot.
bio: Matthias was chosen by lot to replace Judas Iscariot as one of the twelve apostles.

name: Alexander
title: Member of the high-priestly family in Jerusalem
bio: Alexander was a member of the high-priestly family in Jerusalem who was present during Peter and John's interrogation before the Sanhedrin.

name: John
title: A member of the high priest's family
bio: John, a member of the high priest's family, was present during Peter and John's questioning before the Sanhedrin.

name: Barnabas
title: A Levite from Cyprus who accompanied Paul on missionary journeys.

levi.note: Read from the wording of the verse, which doesn't fix the relationship exactly.

bio: Barnabas, whose original name was Joseph or Joses, was a prominent figure in the early Christian church. He was a Levite from the island of Cyprus (Acts 4:36) who sold his land and brought the money to the apostles, demonstrating his generosity and commitment to the faith. Barnabas played a crucial role in introducing the newly converted Paul to the apostles in Jerusalem, vouching for his sincerity (Acts 9:27). The church in Jerusalem later sent Barnabas to Antioch, where he encouraged the believers and brought Paul to minister there (Acts 11:22). Barnabas and Paul were then commissioned by the Holy Spirit to embark on a missionary journey (Acts 13:2), during which they preached the gospel and established churches in various cities. Barnabas was also involved in the dispute concerning the acceptance of Gentile believers and accompanied Paul to the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15). He later separated from Paul due to a disagreement over taking Mark on another journey (Acts 15:36). Barnabas continued his ministry with Mark, while Paul chose Silas as his new companion. In the New Testament epistles, Barnabas is mentioned as a fellow laborer and an example of one who worked for the gospel without relying on financial support from the churches (1 Corinthians 9:6). He was recognized as a pillar of the church alongside James and Peter (Galatians 2:9). Barnabas' ministry was characterized by encouragement, generosity, and a commitment to spreading the gospel message.

name: Ananias
title: Husband of Sapphira, lied about offering proceeds
bio: Ananias, along with his wife Sapphira, lied to the apostles about the proceeds from the sale of their property and faced divine judgment.

name: Sapphira
title: Wife of Ananias, lied to the apostles, died
bio: Sapphira, along with her husband Ananias, lied to the apostles about the proceeds from a property sale and died as a result.

name: Gamaliel
title: Pharisee; teacher of the law; Paul's mentor.
bio: Gamaliel, a respected Pharisee and teacher of the law, was Paul's mentor and advised the Sanhedrin to be cautious in their treatment of the apostles.

name: Theudas
title: Jewish rebel leader killed by Roman authorities
bio: Theudas was a Jewish rebel leader who was killed, and his followers scattered, by the Roman authorities.

name: Judas
title: The Galilean, a Jewish rebel leader
bio: Judas the Galilean led a revolt against the Roman census during the time of Quirinius, governor of Syria.

name: Nicanor
title: One of seven deacons
bio: Nicanor was one of the seven men chosen to assist the apostles in the early Jerusalem church.

name: Nicolaus
title: Proselyte chosen as deacon
bio: Nicolaus was a proselyte from Antioch chosen as one of the seven deacons in the early church.

name: Parmenas
title: One of the seven deacons
bio: Parmenas was one of the seven men chosen by the apostles to serve as deacons in the early church.

name: Philip
title: One of the seven deacons, evangelized in Samaria
bio:
Philip was one of the seven men chosen by the early church in Jerusalem to serve as deacons, responsible for the daily distribution of food to widows (Acts 6:5). After the martyrdom of Stephen, a great persecution arose against the church, and the believers were scattered. Philip went to Samaria and preached the gospel, performing miracles and casting out unclean spirits (Acts 8:4). Many Samaritans believed and were baptized, including Simon the sorcerer (Acts 8:9). 

Philip was then directed by an angel to go south on the road from Jerusalem to Gaza, where he encountered an Ethiopian eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians (Acts 8:26). The eunuch was reading from the book of Isaiah, and Philip explained to him the good news about Jesus (Acts 8:29). The eunuch believed and was baptized by Philip (Acts 8:36). After this, Philip was miraculously transported by the Spirit to Azotus, and he continued preaching the gospel in all the towns until he reached Caesarea (Acts 8:39). 

Later, Philip is mentioned as one of the "seven" and referred to as "Philip the evangelist" (Acts 21:8). He had four unmarried daughters who had the gift of prophecy (Acts 21:9). Paul and his companions stayed with Philip in Caesarea during Paul's final journey to Jerusalem (Acts 21:8).

name: Prochorus
title: One of the seven deacons in Jerusalem
bio: Prochorus, one of the seven men chosen by the early church in Jerusalem to oversee the daily distribution of food to widows.

name: Stephen
title: One of seven deacons, full of faith, performed miracles, martyred.
bio:
Stephen was one of the seven men chosen by the early church in Jerusalem to serve as deacons, responsible for the daily distribution of food to widows (Acts 6:1). He is described as being full of faith, wisdom, and the Holy Spirit (Acts 6:5). 

As Stephen continued to perform wonders and signs among the people, he faced opposition from members of the Synagogue of the Freedmen, who disputed with him (Acts 6:9). However, they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke (Acts 6:10). 

Consequently, they brought false charges against Stephen, accusing him of blasphemy against Moses and God (Acts 6:11). When brought before the Sanhedrin (the Jewish high court), Stephen's face was said to have appeared like the face of an angel (Acts 6:15). 

In his defense, Stephen delivered a powerful speech recounting Israel's history and their rejection of God's prophets, culminating in their rejection of Jesus as the Righteous One (Acts 7:1). He accused his hearers of resisting the Holy Spirit and persecuting the prophets, just as their fathers had done (Acts 7:51). 

Enraged by his words, the members of the Sanhedrin gnashed their teeth at Stephen, but he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:54). When he declared this vision, they dragged him out of the city and stoned him to death, with a young man named Saul (later known as Paul) guarding the garments of those who carried out the execution (Acts 7:56). 

As he was being stoned, Stephen called out to the Lord Jesus to receive his spirit and, echoing Jesus' words on the cross, asked God not to hold this sin against his persecutors (Acts 7:59). Devout men buried Stephen and lamented deeply over him (Acts 8:2). 

Stephen's martyrdom marked a significant turning point in the early church, as it sparked a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem, leading to the dispersion of believers throughout Judea and Samaria (Acts 8:1:19). This dispersion ultimately led to the spread of the gospel beyond Jerusalem, fulfilling Jesus' command to be his witnesses to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8).

name: Timon
title: One of the seven chosen to serve the church
bio: Timon was one of the seven men chosen by the apostles to oversee the daily distribution of food to widows in the early church.

name: Paul
title: Apostle to the Gentiles, author of many NT epistles
bio: Paul, also known as Saul, was one of the most influential figures in early Christianity. He was born in Tarsus as a Roman citizen and trained as a Pharisee under Gamaliel. Initially a persecutor of the church, Paul had a dramatic conversion experience on the road to Damascus, where the risen Jesus appeared to him. After this, he became a zealous preacher of the gospel, undertaking several missionary journeys throughout the Mediterranean world. Paul played a key role in spreading Christianity among the Gentiles and in articulating its theological foundations. He wrote many of the epistles in the New Testament, providing guidance and instruction to the early churches. Paul faced numerous challenges, including opposition from Jewish leaders, internal disputes among believers, and physical hardships. He was eventually arrested and taken to Rome, where tradition holds that he was martyred during the reign of Nero. Paul's life and teachings had a profound impact on the development of Christian thought and practice.

name: Simon
title: Sorcerer in Samaria who tried to buy the Holy Spirit's power.
bio: Simon, often referred to as Simon Magus or Simon the Sorcerer, was a man living in Samaria who practiced sorcery and amazed the people with his magic (Acts 8:9). When Philip came to Samaria preaching the gospel, Simon believed and was baptized along with many others (Acts 8:13). However, when the apostles Peter and John arrived and laid hands on the believers to receive the Holy Spirit, Simon offered them money, wanting to buy the power to impart the Holy Spirit to others (Acts 8:18). Peter sternly rebuked Simon for his attempt to purchase God's gift with money, telling him to repent of his wickedness and pray for forgiveness (Acts 8:20). Simon, frightened by Peter's words, asked the apostles to pray for him (Acts 8:24). This account serves as a warning against the sin of simony (attempting to buy or sell spiritual gifts or offices) and emphasizes that God's gifts cannot be obtained through material means but are freely given by His grace.
meaning: he has heard or obedient one

name: the Ethiopian eunuch
title: an official of queen Candace (Acts 8:27)

name: Candace
title: queen of Ethiopia (Acts 8:27)

name: Ananias
title: Disciple in Damascus, baptized Saul (Paul)
bio: Ananias was a disciple of Jesus Christ living in Damascus. After Saul's dramatic encounter with the risen Christ on the road to Damascus, Saul was left blind and was directed to go into the city to await further instructions. In a vision, the Lord told Ananias to go to the house where Saul was staying and lay hands on him to restore his sight. Initially hesitant due to Saul's reputation as a persecutor of the church, Ananias obeyed the Lord's command. He went to Saul, laid his hands on him, and conveyed the message that Jesus had sent him to restore Saul's sight and to fill him with the Holy Spirit. Ananias then baptized Saul, who later became known as Paul, the great apostle to the Gentiles. Ananias played a crucial role in the early days of Paul's Christian life, demonstrating faith and obedience to God's call.

name: Judas
title: A Christian living on Straight Street in Damascus
bio: Judas was a Christian living on Straight Street in Damascus, where Saul (Paul) stayed after his conversion.

name: Aeneas
title: Paralyzed man in Lydda healed by Peter
bio: Aeneas, paralyzed for eight years, was healed by Peter in Lydda.

name: Tabitha
title: Charitable woman in Joppa whom Peter raised from the dead
bio: Tabitha, also called Dorcas, was a beloved disciple in Joppa known for her charitable works, whom Peter raised from the dead.

name: Simon
title: A tanner in Joppa who hosted Peter.
bio: Simon, a tanner by trade, is mentioned in the book of Acts as a resident of Joppa who hosted the apostle Peter (Acts 9:43). As a tanner, Simon worked with animal hides to produce leather, a profession that was considered unclean by Jewish religious standards. Despite this, Peter stayed with Simon for many days, indicating a growing openness in the early church to interact with Gentiles and those considered unclean. During his stay at Simon's house, Peter received a vision from God in which he was told not to call anything impure that God has made clean (Acts 10:9). This vision prepared Peter for his encounter with Cornelius, a Gentile centurion, whom God had directed to send for Peter (Acts 10:17). Peter's time at Simon the tanner's house marks a significant shift in the early church's understanding of the gospel's inclusivity and the breaking down of barriers between Jews and Gentiles.
meaning: he has heard or obedient one

name: Cornelius
title: Centurion, first Gentile convert to Christianity
bio:
Cornelius was a Roman centurion stationed in Caesarea. He is described as a devout man who feared God, gave alms generously, and prayed regularly (Acts 10:1). Despite his piety, Cornelius was not a convert to Judaism. 

In a vision, an angel instructed Cornelius to send for Peter, who was staying in Joppa (Acts 10:3). Meanwhile, Peter had a vision in which God revealed that he should not consider anything unclean that God had made clean, preparing him to accept Gentile believers (Acts 10:9). 

When Peter arrived at Cornelius' house, Cornelius gathered his relatives and close friends to hear Peter's message (Acts 10:24). As Peter shared the gospel, the Holy Spirit fell upon the Gentile listeners, confirming that God had accepted them (Acts 10:44). This event marked a significant turning point in the early church, as it demonstrated that the gospel was for both Jews and Gentiles. 

Peter then ordered that Cornelius and the other believing Gentiles be baptized (Acts 10:47). The conversion of Cornelius and his household was a pivotal moment in the spread of Christianity, paving the way for the inclusion of Gentiles in the church.

name: Agabus
title: Prophet who predicted famine and Paul's arrest
bio: Agabus, a prophet, foretold a famine and Paul's arrest in Jerusalem.

name: Claudius
title: Roman emperor during Paul's ministry
bio:
Claudius, also referred to as Caesar, was the Roman emperor during a significant portion of Paul's ministry. He is mentioned in several contexts throughout the book of Acts. 

In Acts 11:28, the prophet Agabus foretold a great famine that would occur during the reign of Claudius, which prompted the disciples to send relief to the believers in Judea. 

Acts 18:2 mentions that Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome, which led Aquila and Priscilla to move to Corinth, where they met Paul. 

In Acts 17:7, the accusers of Paul and Silas in Thessalonica claimed that they were acting against the decrees of Caesar, likely referring to Claudius. 

During Paul's trial in Acts 25-26, Claudius is mentioned as the emperor to whom Paul appealed for justice (Acts 25:8). 

In Acts 27:24, an angel told Paul that he must stand before Caesar, referring to Claudius or his successor. 

Finally, in Acts 28:19, Paul stated that he was compelled to appeal to Caesar because of the Jews' opposition. 

These references to Claudius provide historical context for the events in Acts and demonstrate the Roman Empire's significant influence on the early Christian church.

name: Herod
title: A Tetrarch who persecuted the early church.
bio: Herod Agrippa I was the grandson of Herod the Great and ruled as king over Judea, Samaria, and other regions from 41 to 44 AD. In the book of Acts, he is portrayed as a persecutor of the early Christian church. Herod Agrippa I had James, the brother of John, put to death with the sword (Acts 12:1). Seeing that this pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter as well, intending to bring him out for public trial after the Passover (Acts 12:3). However, an angel miraculously freed Peter from prison (Acts 12:6). When Herod Agrippa I discovered Peter's escape, he had the guards executed (Acts 12:19). Later, Herod Agrippa I was involved in a dispute with the people of Tyre and Sidon (Acts 12:20). On the appointed day, he delivered a public address to them, and the people shouted, "This is the voice of a god, not of a man!" (Acts 12:21). Immediately, an angel of the Lord struck him down because he did not give glory to God, and he was eaten by worms and died (Acts 12:23). (Acts 12:1).

name: Mark
title: Cousin of Barnabas, companion of Paul, author of Gospel.
bio: Mark, also known as John Mark, was a prominent figure in the early Christian church. He was the son of Mary, whose house in Jerusalem served as a meeting place for the believers (Acts 12:12). Mark was also the cousin of Barnabas (Colossians 4:10) and accompanied Paul and Barnabas on their first missionary journey (Acts 12:25). However, he left them at Perga and returned to Jerusalem (Acts 13:13), which later caused a disagreement between Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:37). Despite this, Mark remained active in ministry, as evidenced by Paul's later references to him as a fellow worker (Philemon 1:24; 2 Timothy 4:11). He also worked closely with Peter, who referred to him as "my son Mark" (1 Peter 5:13). Tradition holds that Mark wrote the Gospel that bears his name based on Peter's teachings, making it one of the earliest written accounts of Jesus' life and ministry.

name: Mary
title: Mother of John Mark; hosted prayer meeting.
bio: Mary, the mother of John Mark, hosted a prayer meeting in her house.
meaning: [variously] bitterness; plump one; wished-for child; one who loves or is loved

name: Rhoda
title: Servant girl in the house of Mary
bio: Rhoda was a servant girl in the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, who recognized Peter's voice at the door.

name: Blastus
title: Herod's chamberlain who helped the people of Tyre and Sidon
bio: Blastus, Herod's chamberlain, was persuaded by the people of Tyre and Sidon to help them gain the king's favor.

name: Lucius
title: Prophet and teacher in the church at Antioch.
bio: Lucius of Cyrene was a prophet and teacher in the church at Antioch who was involved in sending Paul and Barnabas on their first missionary journey.

name: Manaen
title: Prophet and teacher in the church at Antioch.
bio: Manaen, a prophet and teacher, was part of the church at Antioch.

name: Simeon
title: Prophet and teacher in the church at Antioch.
bio: Simeon, also called Niger, was a prophet and teacher in the church at Antioch who was involved in sending Paul and Barnabas on their first missionary journey.

name: Bar-jesus
title: A Jewish sorcerer who opposed Paul and Barnabas.
bio: Bar-Jesus, also known as Elymas, was a Jewish sorcerer who tried to hinder Paul and Barnabas' ministry.

name: Sergius Paulus
title: Proconsul of Cyprus, converted under Paul's ministry
bio: Sergius Paulus, the proconsul of Cyprus, was an intelligent man who sought to hear the word of God and believed after witnessing Paul's confrontation with Elymas the sorcerer.

name: Judas
title: A prophet and leader in the Jerusalem church
bio: Judas, also known as Barsabbas, was a prophet and respected leader in the Jerusalem church who accompanied Paul and Barnabas to Antioch.

name: Silas
title: Prominent member of the Jerusalem church, companion of Paul.
bio:
Silas, also known as Silvanus, was a significant figure in the early Christian church, particularly in his role as a companion of the apostle Paul. He is first mentioned in Acts 15:22 as a prominent member of the Jerusalem church, along with Judas Barsabbas, chosen to accompany Paul and Barnabas to Antioch to deliver the decision of the Jerusalem Council regarding Gentile believers. 

Described as a prophet (Acts 15:32), Silas played a vital role in encouraging and strengthening the churches. After parting ways with Barnabas, Paul chose Silas as his new companion for his second missionary journey (Acts 15:40). Together, they traveled through Syria, Cilicia, and various cities in Asia Minor, preaching the gospel and establishing churches. 

In Philippi, Paul and Silas were imprisoned for their ministry but were miraculously freed by an earthquake (Acts 16:19). They continued their journey, ministering in Thessalonica, Berea, and Corinth (Acts 17:1:5). Silas remained with Paul in Corinth for an extended period, helping him establish the church there. 

In addition to his missionary work, Silas is also mentioned as a co-author of some of Paul's epistles, specifically 1 and 2 Thessalonians (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1). He is also referred to as Silvanus in 2 Corinthians 1:19 and 1 Peter 5:12, where he is described as a faithful brother. 

Silas' dedication to the gospel, his leadership in the early church, and his partnership with Paul make him an important figure in the spread of Christianity during the first century.

name: Timothy
title: Paul's young disciple and co-worker

eunice.note: Named in the same passage, but Scripture doesn't state this word for word.

father-of-timothy-act-16-1.note: Read from the wording of the verse, which doesn't fix the relationship exactly.

bio: Timothy was a young disciple and close companion of the Apostle Paul. He is mentioned frequently in the New Testament, both in the book of Acts and in Paul's epistles. Timothy was from Lystra, the son of a Greek father and a Jewish mother named Eunice (Acts 16:1). He was well-respected by the believers in his hometown and in Iconium (Acts 16:2). Paul invited Timothy to join him on his missionary journeys, and he became a valuable assistant and co-worker (Acts 16:3). Paul referred to Timothy as his "true son in the faith" (1 Timothy 1:2) and sent him on important missions to churches in Macedonia, Achaia, and Ephesus (Acts 19:22; 1 Corinthians 4:17; Philippians 2:19). Timothy was with Paul during his first Roman imprisonment and is named as a co-sender of several of Paul's letters (Philippians 1:1; Colossians 1:1; Philemon 1:1). Paul also wrote two personal letters to Timothy, providing guidance and encouragement for his pastoral ministry (1 Timothy 1:2; 2 Timothy 1:2). These letters, along with the letter to Titus, are known as the Pastoral Epistles. According to Hebrews 13:23, Timothy was imprisoned at some point but later released. Tradition holds that Timothy served as the bishop of Ephesus in his later years. Timothy's life and ministry exemplify the importance of mentoring, discipleship, and faithful service in the early church.

name: Father of Timothy
title: Father of Timothy - Greek man; husband of Eunice
bio: Timothy's father was a Greek man, and his mother was a believing Jewish woman named Eunice.

name: Lydia
title: Seller of purple goods; converted by Paul in Philippi
bio: Lydia, a seller of purple goods from Thyatira, was converted by Paul in Philippi and hosted the church in her home.

name: Jason
title: Paul's host in Thessalonica; relative of Paul
bio: Jason is mentioned in Acts 17:5 as the host of Paul and Silas during their visit to Thessalonica. He provided lodging for the missionaries while they preached in the city. However, their presence caused an uproar among the Jews who were jealous of Paul's success in converting people to Christianity. A mob formed and attacked Jason's house, seeking to bring Paul and Silas before the city authorities. When they could not find the missionaries, they dragged Jason and some other believers before the city officials, accusing them of harboring those who were defying Caesar's decrees. The officials took security from Jason and the others before releasing them. In Romans 16:21, Paul mentions a Jason as one of his fellow workers and relatives who send greetings to the church in Rome. It is unclear whether this is the same Jason who hosted Paul in Thessalonica, but the shared name and association with Paul suggest that it could be the same person.

name: Damaris
title: Woman who believed Paul's message in Athens
bio: Damaris was a woman who believed Paul's message in Athens and joined him.

name: Dionysius
title: Areopagite who believed Paul's message in Athens
bio: Dionysius the Areopagite was one of the people who believed Paul's message when he preached in Athens.

name: Aquila
title: Jewish Christian tentmaker, co-worker with Paul
bio:
Aquila was a Jewish Christian from Pontus who, along with his wife Priscilla, played a significant role in the early church. He is first mentioned in the book of Acts as a tentmaker who had recently come to Corinth from Italy due to the emperor Claudius' decree expelling all Jews from Rome. Paul, also a tentmaker, stayed and worked with Aquila and Priscilla during his time in Corinth. 

When Paul left Corinth, Aquila and Priscilla accompanied him to Ephesus. There, they met Apollos, an eloquent Jewish Christian from Alexandria who knew only the baptism of John. Aquila and Priscilla took Apollos aside and explained to him the way of God more accurately, enabling him to continue his effective ministry. 

In Paul's letter to the Romans, he sends greetings to Aquila and Priscilla, commending them as his co-workers in Christ Jesus who risked their lives for him. Paul also mentions that the church met in their house, indicating their significant role in hosting and supporting the local Christian community. 

Aquila and Priscilla are mentioned again in Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, where he sends greetings from them and the church that meets at their house. Finally, in Paul's second letter to Timothy, he asks Timothy to greet Aquila and Priscilla, demonstrating their ongoing involvement in the ministry and their close relationship with Paul and his associates.

name: Priscilla
title: Early Christian teacher; wife of Aquila
bio: Priscilla, also referred to as Prisca, was a prominent Jewish Christian woman in the early church. She is consistently mentioned alongside her husband, Aquila, suggesting that they worked together as a team in ministry. Priscilla and Aquila were originally from Rome but had been forced to leave due to the emperor Claudius' edict expelling the Jews (Acts 18:2). They settled in Corinth, where they met the apostle Paul and worked with him as tentmakers (Acts 18:3). When Paul left Corinth, Priscilla and Aquila accompanied him to Ephesus (Acts 18:18). In Ephesus, they encountered Apollos, a learned Jewish Christian, and instructed him more accurately in the way of God (Acts 18:26). This event highlights Priscilla's knowledge of the Scriptures and her active role in teaching and discipleship. Priscilla and Aquila also hosted a church in their home, both in Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:19) and later in Rome (Romans 16:3). Paul's warm greetings to the couple in his letters testify to their close friendship and partnership in the gospel ministry (Romans 16:3; 2 Timothy 4:19). Priscilla's example demonstrates the significant contributions of women in the early spread of Christianity and their active roles in the life of the church.

name: Justus
title: Titius Justus, a Gentile believer who hosted Paul in Corinth
bio: Titius Justus, a Gentile worshiper of God, hosted Paul in Corinth after he left the synagogue.

name: Crispus
title: Synagogue leader in Corinth who believed in Jesus
bio: Crispus, the synagogue leader in Corinth, believed in Jesus and was baptized by Paul.

name: Gallio
title: Roman proconsul of Achaia; refused to judge Paul.
bio: Gallio, the Roman proconsul of Achaia, refused to judge Paul when the Jews brought charges against him in Corinth.

name: Sosthenes
title: Synagogue ruler in Corinth, co-sender of 1 Corinthians.
bio: Sosthenes was a synagogue ruler in Corinth who was beaten by a mob and later became a co-sender of Paul's first letter to the Corinthians.

name: Apollos
title: Eloquent Jewish Christian from Alexandria, co-worker with Paul
bio:
Apollos was a prominent Jewish Christian from Alexandria, known for his eloquence, knowledge of the Scriptures, and effectiveness in preaching the gospel. He is first mentioned in the book of Acts as a learned man who spoke with great fervor and taught about Jesus accurately, though he knew only the baptism of John. After receiving further instruction from Priscilla and Aquila in Ephesus, Apollos went to Achaia and greatly helped the believers there, vigorously refuting the Jews in public debate and proving from the Scriptures that Jesus was the Messiah. 

In Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, Apollos is mentioned as one of the leaders that some of the Corinthian believers were aligning themselves with, alongside Paul and Cephas (Peter). Paul clarifies that both he and Apollos are merely servants through whom the Corinthians came to believe, each serving the role God had assigned to them. Paul planted, Apollos watered, but God made it grow. Paul also mentions Apollos as a positive example when discussing the need for humility and unity among believers. 

Later, in Paul's letter to Titus, Apollos is mentioned again as someone Paul encourages Titus to help on his journey, together with Zenas the lawyer. This suggests that Apollos continued to be actively involved in ministry and was a valued co-worker in spreading the gospel message.

name: Tyrannus
title: Ephesian teacher who hosted Paul's discussions
bio: Tyrannus was a teacher in Ephesus who allowed Paul to use his lecture hall for daily discussions about the gospel.

name: Sceva
title: Jewish chief priest whose seven sons attempted to exorcise demons
bio: Sceva was a Jewish chief priest whose seven sons attempted to exorcise demons in the name of Jesus, as mentioned in the book of Acts.

name: Erastus
title: Companion of Paul; served as city treasurer in Corinth.
bio: Erastus was a companion of Paul who served as the city treasurer in Corinth.

name: Demetrius
title: Silversmith who opposed Paul in Ephesus
bio: Demetrius, a silversmith in Ephesus, stirred up opposition against Paul because his preaching threatened the business of making shrines of Artemis.

name: Aristarchus
title: Macedonian companion of Paul, fellow prisoner
bio:
Aristarchus was a Macedonian Christian from Thessalonica who became a close companion and fellow worker of the apostle Paul. He is mentioned several times in the New Testament, providing insight into his dedication to the gospel and his support of Paul's ministry. 

In Acts 19:29, during the riot in Ephesus, Aristarchus and Gaius are described as Paul's traveling companions who were seized by the mob. This incident highlights the dangers faced by early Christians as they spread the gospel message. 

Aristarchus is later mentioned as one of the delegates who accompanied Paul on his journey to Jerusalem (Acts 20:4), demonstrating his commitment to supporting Paul and the church. In Acts 27:2, we learn that Aristarchus was also with Paul during his voyage to Rome as a prisoner, further emphasizing his loyalty and willingness to face hardships for the sake of the gospel. 

In Paul's letters, Aristarchus is described as a fellow prisoner (Col. Acts 4:10) and a fellow worker (Phm. Acts 1:24). These references suggest that Aristarchus not only traveled with Paul but also shared in his sufferings and labored alongside him in ministry. 

Aristarchus' consistent presence in Paul's life, from his missionary journeys to his imprisonment, testifies to his unwavering faith and dedication to the spread of the gospel. His example serves as an encouragement to believers to remain faithful and committed to serving Christ, even in the face of adversity.

name: Gaius
title: Macedonian; Paul's traveling companion; caught in Ephesian riot.
bio: Gaius, a Macedonian and traveling companion of Paul, was seized along with Aristarchus during the riot in Ephesus.

name: Alexander
title: Jew put forward by the crowd in Ephesus
bio: Alexander was a Jew whom the crowd put forward during the riot in Ephesus, but they shouted him down when they realized he was a Jew.

name: Gaius
title: Derbean; accompanied Paul on his journey to Jerusalem.
bio: Gaius of Derbe accompanied Paul on his journey from Greece to Jerusalem, along with several others.

name: Pyrrhus
title: A Berean who accompanied Paul to Asia
bio: Pyrrhus was a Berean who accompanied Paul on his journey to Asia.

name: Secundus
title: Thessalonian believer who accompanied Paul
bio: Secundus was a Thessalonian believer who accompanied Paul on his journey.

name: Sopater
title: Companion of Paul from Berea, greeted the Roman church.

pyrrhus-1.note: Named in the same passage, but Scripture doesn't state this word for word.

bio: Sopater (or Sosipater) was a companion of Paul from Berea who accompanied him on his journey to Jerusalem and later sent greetings to the church in Rome.

name: Trophimus
title: Gentile Christian from Ephesus, companion of Paul
bio: Trophimus was a Gentile Christian from Ephesus who accompanied Paul on his missionary journeys and was falsely accused of defiling the temple in Jerusalem.

name: Tychicus
title: Faithful companion and messenger of Paul
bio: Tychicus was a faithful companion and fellow worker of the Apostle Paul, mentioned several times in the New Testament (Acts 20:4; Ephesians 6:21; Colossians 4:7; 2 Timothy 4:12; Titus 3:12). He was from the province of Asia (modern-day western Turkey) and accompanied Paul on his third missionary journey. Paul entrusted Tychicus with important missions, sending him as a messenger to the churches in Ephesus (Ephesians 6:21) and Colossae (Colossians 4:7) to deliver letters and bring news of Paul's circumstances. In these letters, Paul describes Tychicus as a beloved brother, faithful minister, and fellow servant in the Lord. Later, Paul sent Tychicus to Ephesus to relieve Timothy (2 Timothy 4:12) and planned to send him to Crete to assist Titus (Titus 3:12). Tychicus' frequent appearances in Paul's letters and his role as a trusted messenger demonstrate his significance in the early church and his close relationship with the apostle.

name: Eutychus
title: Young man in Troas; fell from window; restored by Paul.
bio: Eutychus was a young man in Troas who fell from a window and was restored to life by Paul.

name: Mnason
title: A Cypriot disciple who hosted Paul in Jerusalem.
bio: Mnason, an early disciple from Cyprus, provided lodging for Paul and his companions when they arrived in Jerusalem.

name: Ananias
title: High priest during Paul's trial
bio: Ananias, the high priest, presided over Paul's trial and ordered him to be struck on the mouth for his defense.

name: Felix
title: Roman governor of Judea; heard Paul's case.
bio: Felix was a Roman procurator (governor) of Judea who served from approximately 52 to 60 AD. He is mentioned in the book of Acts in connection with the apostle Paul's imprisonment and trial. Paul was brought before Felix in Caesarea after being accused by the Jewish leaders of being a troublemaker and inciting riots (Acts 23:24). During the hearing, Paul defended himself against the charges and spoke about his faith in Christ (Acts 24:10). Felix, who was well-informed about Christianity, postponed making a decision and kept Paul in custody, hoping to receive a bribe from him (Acts 24:22). Felix also heard Paul speak about righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, which caused him to be afraid (Acts 24:25). However, Felix left Paul in prison for two years until his successor, Porcius Festus, took office (Acts 24:27). The account of Paul's interaction with Felix highlights the challenges faced by early Christians in the face of Roman authority and the corruption within the judicial system.

name: Lysias
title: Roman commander who rescued Paul from a Jewish mob
bio: Claudius Lysias, the Roman commander in Jerusalem, rescued Paul from a Jewish mob and sent him to Felix.

name: Tertullus
title: Lawyer who accused Paul before Governor Felix
bio: Tertullus was a lawyer hired by the Jewish authorities to accuse Paul before the Roman governor Felix.

name: Drusilla
title: Jewish wife of Felix, the Roman governor
bio: Drusilla, the Jewish wife of Felix, the Roman governor, was present when Paul spoke to Felix about faith in Christ.

name: Festus
title: Roman governor of Judea; heard Paul's case; sent him to Rome.
bio: Porcius Festus was a Roman procurator (governor) of Judea who succeeded Felix around 60 AD (Acts 24:27). He is mentioned in the book of Acts in relation to the apostle Paul's ongoing legal case. Upon taking office, Festus was confronted with the charges against Paul that had been left unresolved by Felix (Acts 25:1). Festus, wanting to do the Jews a favor, asked Paul if he would be willing to go to Jerusalem for trial, but Paul appealed to Caesar, asserting his rights as a Roman citizen (Acts 25:9). Festus, unsure how to handle the case, consulted with King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice, who came to Caesarea to pay their respects to the new governor (Acts 25:13). Paul was brought before Festus, Agrippa, and Bernice to present his defense (Acts 25:23:32). After hearing Paul's testimony, Festus exclaimed that Paul's great learning had driven him insane (Acts 26:24). Agrippa, however, believed that Paul could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar (Acts 26:32). Festus then sent Paul to Rome for trial, as he had requested (Acts 27:1). The account of Festus's involvement in Paul's case illustrates the complexities of the Roman legal system and the challenges faced by early Christians in navigating it.

name: Agrippa
title: Tetrarch who heard Paul's defense in Caesarea
bio:
Agrippa, also known as Herod Agrippa II, was the great-grandson of Herod the Great. He ruled over various territories in Judea during the time of Paul's imprisonment in Caesarea. Agrippa, along with his sister Bernice, visited Festus, the Roman governor. Festus presented Paul's case to Agrippa, who expressed his desire to hear Paul. (Acts 25:13) 

The next day, Paul appeared before Agrippa and Bernice and made his defense, recounting his conversion and ministry. Agrippa, familiar with Jewish customs and controversies, listened intently. Paul appealed to Agrippa's belief in the prophets and challenged him to believe in Christ. Agrippa replied, "Do you think that in such a short time you can persuade me to be a Christian?" (Acts 26:1).

name: Bernice
title: Jewish princess, sister of King Agrippa II
bio: Bernice, a Jewish princess and sister of King Agrippa II, heard Paul's defense.

name: Julius
title: A centurion of the Augustan Cohort
bio: Julius, a centurion of the Augustan Cohort, was responsible for escorting Paul to Rome and showed him kindness during the journey.

name: Publius
title: Chief official of Malta who hosted Paul
bio: Publius, the chief official of Malta, who hosted Paul and his companions for three days after their shipwreck on the island.

name: Phoebe
title: Deacon of the church in Cenchreae
bio: Phoebe, a deacon of the church in Cenchreae, whom Paul commended to the believers in Rome.

name: Epaenetus
title: A believer in Asia and beloved by Paul.
bio: Epaenetus was the first convert to Christ in Asia and was beloved by Paul.

name: Mary
title: A woman who worked hard for the church in Rome.
bio: Mary was a woman who worked very hard for the church in Rome.
meaning: [variously] bitterness; plump one; wished-for child; one who loves or is loved

name: Andronicus
title: Fellow prisoner with Paul, outstanding among the apostles
bio: Andronicus, along with Junia, was a fellow prisoner with Paul and was noted as outstanding among the apostles.

name: Junia
title: A prominent apostle and relative of Paul
bio: Junia, along with Andronicus, was recognized as a prominent apostle and a relative of Paul who had been imprisoned with him.

name: Ampliatus
title: Believer greeted by Paul in Rome
bio: Ampliatus, a beloved fellow believer greeted by Paul in his letter to the Romans.

name: Stachys
title: Believer in Rome, greeted by Paul as a beloved friend.
bio: Stachys was a believer in Rome whom Paul greeted as his beloved friend.

name: Urbanus
title: Christian in Rome greeted by Paul
bio: Urbanus was a Christian in Rome whom Paul called a fellow worker in Christ and to whom he sent greetings.

name: Apelles
title: Approved in Christ, greeted by Paul
bio: Apelles, described as "approved in Christ," was among those greeted by Paul in his letter to the Romans.

name: Aristobulus
title: Believer in Rome, greeted by Paul
bio: Paul sends greetings to those who belong to the household of Aristobulus, suggesting that Aristobulus was a prominent believer in Rome.

name: Herodion
title: A relative of Paul in Rome.
bio: Herodion was a relative of Paul in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings.

name: Narcissus
title: Christian in Rome with a household
bio: Narcissus was likely a wealthy Christian in Rome with a household of believers.

name: Persis
title: Female Christian in Rome greeted by Paul
bio: Persis, a beloved female Christian in Rome whom Paul greeted in his letter to the Romans.

name: Tryphaena
title: Christian woman in Rome greeted by Paul
bio: Tryphaena was a Christian woman in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings in his letter to the Romans.

name: Tryphosa
title: Christian woman in Rome greeted by Paul
bio: Tryphosa was a Christian woman in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings in his letter to the Romans.

name: Rufus
title: Believer in Rome, son of Paul's "mother"
bio: Rufus was a believer in Rome, chosen in the Lord, whose mother had also been a mother figure to Paul.

name: Asyncritus
title: Believer in Rome greeted by Paul
bio: Asyncritus was a believer in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings (Romans 16:14).

name: Hermes
title: A Christian in Rome greeted by Paul.
bio: Hermes was a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings in his letter to the Romans.

name: Hermas
title: A Christian in Rome greeted by Paul.
bio: Hermas was a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings in his letter to the Romans.

name: Patrobas
title: Believer in Rome greeted by Paul
bio: Patrobas, a believer in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings.

name: Phlegon
title: Believer in Rome greeted by Paul
bio: Phlegon, a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings in his letter to the Romans.

name: Julia
title: A Christian woman greeted by Paul in Romans
bio: Julia, along with Philologus and Nereus, was greeted by Paul in his letter to the Romans.

name: Nereus
title: A Christian in Rome greeted by Paul.
bio: Nereus was a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings in his letter to the Romans.

name: Olympas
title: Believer greeted by Paul
bio: Olympas was a believer in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings.

name: Philologus
title: Believer in Rome greeted by Paul
bio: Philologus, a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings in his letter to the Romans.

name: Tertius
title: Paul's scribe who wrote the Epistle to the Romans
bio: Tertius served as Paul's scribe, writing down the Epistle to the Romans.

name: Gaius
title: Corinthian believer; host to Paul and the church.
bio: Gaius, a Corinthian believer baptized by Paul, hosted Paul and the whole church in his home.

name: Quartus
title: A Christian brother in Corinth who sent greetings to Rome
bio: Quartus, a Christian brother in Corinth, sent greetings to the believers in Rome through Paul's letter.

name: Chloe
title: Believer whose household reported divisions in Corinthian church
bio: Chloe's household informed Paul about divisions in the Corinthian church.

name: Stephanas
title: Corinthian believer, baptized by Paul, sent to visit him.
bio: Stephanas was a believer from Corinth who, along with his household, was baptized by Paul and later visited Paul to provide support and encouragement.

name: Achaicus
title: A Corinthian Christian who visited Paul.
bio: Achaicus, along with Stephanas and Fortunatus, visited Paul from Corinth.

name: Fortunatus
title: Corinthian Christian; visited Paul in Ephesus.
bio: Fortunatus was a Corinthian Christian who, along with Stephanas and Achaicus, visited Paul in Ephesus and refreshed his spirit.

name: Titus
title: Gentile convert and companion of Paul
bio: Titus was a Gentile convert and a close companion of the Apostle Paul. He is mentioned several times in Paul's epistles, particularly in 2 Corinthians and the letter addressed to him, the Epistle to Titus. Titus was one of Paul's trusted delegates and was involved in his ministry to the churches. Paul refers to Titus as his "true son in the faith" (Titus 1:4), indicating a close spiritual relationship. Titus accompanied Paul to Jerusalem for the council that discussed the inclusion of Gentiles in the church (Galatians 2:1). He was not compelled to be circumcised, which supported Paul's stance that Gentile converts did not need to adhere to Jewish law. Titus played a significant role in Paul's relationship with the church in Corinth. He was sent by Paul to Corinth to address issues within the church and to encourage the believers (2 Corinthians 7:6). Titus' visit brought comfort and reassurance to Paul regarding the Corinthians' response to his earlier letter. Paul also entrusted Titus with the task of collecting an offering for the believers in Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 8:6). The Epistle to Titus, written by Paul, provides insight into Titus' role as a church leader. Paul had left Titus in Crete to oversee the churches there, appointing elders and dealing with false teachers (Titus 1:5). The letter offers guidance on sound doctrine, qualifications for church leaders, and the importance of good works. According to 2 Timothy 4:10, Titus later traveled to Dalmatia (modern-day Croatia). Church tradition holds that Titus served as the first bishop of Crete. Titus' life exemplifies the important role that Gentile converts played in the early church and the trust Paul placed in them as fellow ministers of the gospel.

name: Aretas
title: King of the Nabataeans in Damascus
bio: Aretas, the king of the Nabataeans, governed Damascus and tried to arrest Paul.

name: Epaphroditus
title: A messenger and minister to Paul from Philippi.
bio: Epaphroditus was a beloved brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier who ministered to Paul's needs on behalf of the Philippians.

name: Euodia
title: Christian woman in Philippi; urged by Paul to reconcile.
bio: Euodia was a Christian woman in Philippi whom Paul urged to reconcile with Syntyche.

name: Syntyche
title: Woman in the Philippian church whom Paul exhorted
bio: Syntyche was a prominent woman in Philippi whom Paul urged to reconcile with Euodia.

name: Clement
title: Fellow laborer with Paul in the gospel
bio: Clement was a fellow laborer with Paul, whose name was in the Book of Life.

name: Nero
title: Roman emperor
bio: Nero was likely the Roman emperor during Paul's final imprisonment.

name: Epaphras
title: A faithful minister and fellow servant of Paul.
bio: Epaphras was a faithful minister of Christ and a fellow prisoner with Paul, who labored in prayer for the Colossians.

name: Onesimus
title: Runaway slave, convert of Paul
bio: Onesimus was a runaway slave who became a Christian through Paul's ministry and was the subject of Paul's letter to Philemon.

name: Justus
title: Jesus Justus, a Jewish believer who supported Paul
bio: Jesus, also called Justus, was one of the few Jewish believers who supported Paul during his imprisonment.

name: Demas
title: Companion of Paul who later deserted him
bio: Demas was a companion of Paul who later deserted him because he loved the world.

name: Luke
title: Physician; companion of Paul; author of Luke and Acts
bio: Luke, a physician and companion of Paul, was the author of the Gospel of Luke and the Book of Acts.

name: Nympha
title: Hosted a church in her house
bio: Nympha was a woman who hosted a church in her house in Laodicea.

name: Archippus
title: Fellow soldier and minister in Colossae
bio: Archippus, addressed as a fellow soldier by Paul, was urged to complete the ministry he had received in the Lord.

name: Alexander
title: Opponent of Paul, along with Hymenaeus
bio: Alexander, along with Hymenaeus, was an opponent of Paul's teaching and was handed over to Satan by Paul.

name: Hymenaeus
title: A man who rejected faith and good conscience.
bio: Hymenaeus was a man who had rejected the faith and was handed over to Satan by Paul so that he might learn not to blaspheme.

name: Eunice
title: Mother of Timothy; a Jewish believer.
bio: Eunice was the mother of Timothy and a Jewish believer.

name: Lois
title: Grandmother of Timothy; commended for her faith
bio: Lois, the grandmother of Timothy, was commended by Paul for her sincere faith.

name: Hermogenes
title: A believer who deserted Paul in Asia.
bio: Hermogenes was one of the believers in Asia who deserted Paul during his imprisonment.

name: Phygelus
title: Believer who deserted Paul in Asia
bio: Phygelus, along with Hermogenes, was mentioned by Paul as having deserted him during his ministry in Asia.

name: Onesiphorus
title: Friend and supporter of Paul
bio: Onesiphorus was a friend of Paul who often refreshed him and was not ashamed of his imprisonment.

name: Philetus
title: False teacher who opposed Paul
bio: Philetus, along with Hymenaeus, was a false teacher who had strayed from the truth and taught that the resurrection had already taken place.

name: Jambres
title: Egyptian magician who opposed Moses
bio: Jambres was an Egyptian magician who, along with Jannes, opposed Moses.

name: Jannes
title: Egyptian magician who opposed Moses
bio: Jannes was an Egyptian magician who, along with Jambres, opposed Moses.

name: Crescens
title: Companion of Paul who went to Galatia
bio: Crescens, a companion of Paul, went to Galatia during Paul's imprisonment.

name: Carpus
title: Paul's friend in Troas
bio: Carpus was a friend of Paul in Troas, with whom Paul left his cloak, books, and parchments.

name: Claudia
title: Believer in Rome who sent greetings to Timothy
bio: Claudia, along with others, sent greetings to Timothy in Paul's letter.

name: Eubulus
title: Greeted by Paul in his letter to Timothy.
bio: Eubulus was a Christian who sent greetings to Timothy through Paul's letter.

name: Linus
title: Christian in Rome; greeted by Paul
bio: Linus, a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings.

name: Pudens
title: Christian in Rome who greeted Timothy
bio: Pudens, a Christian in Rome who sent greetings to Timothy through Paul's letter.

name: Artemas
title: Companion of Paul, potential replacement for Titus
bio: Artemas was a companion of Paul who could potentially replace Titus in Crete (Titus 3:12).

name: Zenas
title: Christian lawyer whom Paul commended
bio: Zenas, a lawyer, was commended by Paul and was to be sent on his journey with Apollos.

name: Philemon
title: Recipient of Paul's letter, Colossian slave owner
bio: Philemon, a Christian from Colossae to whom Paul wrote a letter appealing for the reconciliation with his runaway slave, Onesimus.

name: Apphia
title: Recipient of Paul's letter to Philemon
bio: Apphia, likely a member of Philemon's household, was one of the recipients of Paul's letter to Philemon.

name: Gaius
title: Recipient of John's third epistle; commended for his faithfulness.
bio: Gaius, the recipient of John's third epistle, was commended for his faithfulness to the truth and his hospitality to traveling missionaries.

name: Diotrephes
title: Church leader who opposed John
bio: Diotrephes was a church leader who loved to be first and refused to welcome John and his companions.

name: Antipas
title: Faithful martyr in Pergamum
bio: Antipas, described as Christ's faithful witness, was martyred in Pergamum, where Satan's throne was said to be.

name: Death
title: the rider of the pale/ashen horse (Revelation 6:8)

name: Abaddon
title: king over the locusts of Revelation 9, the angel of the abyss (Revelation 9:11)
